Daily</span></a><div class="_8nrv"><span class="x8t9es0 xw23nyj xo1l8bm x63nzvj x6lvj10 xq9mrsl x1h4wwuj xeuugli"><div class="_4ik4 _4ik5" style="-webkit-line-clamp: 2;"><div><span class="x14vqqas"><strong>Sponsored</strong></span><span><strong></strong></span></div></div></span></div></div></div></div></div><div class="x1plvlek xryxfnj"><div class="_7jyr _a25-"><span class="x8t9es0 xw23nyj xo1l8bm x63nzvj x108nfp6 xq9mrsl x1h4wwuj xeuugli"><div tabindex="0" role="button"><div class="_4ik4 _4ik5" style="line-height: 16px; max-height: 112px; -webkit-line-clamp: 7;"><div style="white-space: pre-wrap;"><span>My father took MiraLAX every morning for twelve years. He died at 63 of complications of chronic constipation.<br><br>Three months ago I sat in the same kind of exam chair he used to sit in, and a doctor reached for the same prescription.<br><br>I almost said yes — until my husband asked the one question that would have saved my father's life.<br><br>I'm Diane. I'm 45.<br><br>My father has been gone twelve years now. The winter our youngest was still small.<br><br>The death certificate said "complications of chronic constipation." I didn't really understand what that meant until I read the hospital summary on the drive home from the funeral.<br><br>He was a quiet man. A shop teacher in Millbrook for thirty-one years. After he retired he built cabinets out of the garage.<br><br>He worked with his hands. He built the kitchen table I grew up eating at.<br><br>The MiraLAX showed up on his counter the year I turned 30.<br><br>His doctor called it the gold standard. Gentle. Non-habit-forming. "You'll probably need it long-term, but that's fine."<br><br>For twelve years he scooped the white powder into his orange juice every morning.<br><br>He'd say "regular as a clock" at Sunday dinner. Like a small joke. I believed him.<br><br>The dependency came inside the first year. Miss a day, nothing moved. "I guess I just need it now."<br><br>By year three, one scoop wasn't enough. The doctor moved him to two. "Your body adjusted. Normal."<br><br>By year five they added magnesium citrate, three times a week. "Just to keep things moving."<br><br>And the bloating.<br><br>By the end his belly swelled every afternoon like he was carrying a basketball. He stopped tucking his shirts in. He started wearing loose flannel buttoned over it.<br><br>The brain fog crept in around year four. Losing conversations mid-sentence. Asleep at the table by seven.<br><br>The exhaustion wasn't tiredness. It was a poisoning kind of tired.<br><br>He died at 63.<br><br>Bowel obstruction. An impaction that had been building for months behind the managed output. Perforation. Sepsis.<br><br>Twelve years of managed movements. Twelve years of escalating doses. Twelve years of his doctor saying "the MiraLAX is working."<br><br>And he died of the thing they were managing.<br><br>I started slipping around the time my fortieth birthday came and went.<br><br>Every other day. Then every third. Then every fourth.<br><br>By 42 it was every four to five days at best.<br><br>The bloat showed up by dinner like a guest who would not leave. I look six months pregnant by eight o'clock. I stopped wearing the green dress. Stopped tucking shirts in.<br><br>Pebble stools when I went at all. Rabbit pellets.<br><br>The strain hour at six a.m. Door locked. Knees pulled up to my chest. Ninety minutes while the rest of the house slept.<br><br>Blood on the paper one morning. I cried in the bathroom and then I went to work.<br><br>I dread thinking about when I will poop.<br><br>I stopped saying that out loud somewhere around my fortieth birthday. Because I could hear my mother saying it about my father.<br><br>One night I stood in front of my own bathroom drawer and made myself list it out loud.<br><br>MiraLAX. White powder, orange juice in the morning.<br><br>Metamucil. Three orange tubs stacked in the back.<br><br>Magnesium citrate. The soda bottle I'd chug Sunday nights. Tastes like grapefruit lighter fluid.<br><br>Magnesium glycinate. The calm one. Didn't move anything.<br><br>Senna. The brown tablets. The whip I'd take when I had a flight Tuesday.<br><br>Dulcolax suppositories. The emergency drawer.<br><br>Milk of Magnesia. Chalky nightly chugs. Stopped working after a few rounds.<br><br>Align. Thirty dollars a month for six months. Three good weeks. Then nothing.<br><br>Smooth Move tea. The kettle on at nine every Sunday.<br><br>Prune juice. Every morning until I gagged at the sight of the bottle.<br><br>Triphala. Two weeks of working, then nothing.<br><br>Fiber gummies. Made the bloat worse.<br><br>The squatty potty under the sink.<br><br>A clean colonoscopy at 41. Nothing remarkable.<br><br>I closed the drawer.<br><br>Half of those were in my father's cabinet too.<br><br>I'd been buying them my whole life and not seeing it.<br><br>This past winter we started clearing out my father's garage workshop to sell the house.<br><br>The pegboard of hand tools still hung where he left it. The wall calendar was still on the month he died.<br><br>On the workbench, behind a coffee can of screws, I found a near-empty tub of MiraLAX.<br><br>The scoop was still in it. Worn smooth from twelve years of mornings.<br><br>I held it.<br><br>Set it down.<br><br>Drove home and booked the first appointment with my doctor. Made a note in my phone to actually go this time.<br><br>Three weeks later I was in the chair.<br><br>My old doctor had retired. This was someone new, in the same kind of room my father had used for fifteen years.<br><br>He listened for six minutes.<br><br>"You've tried a lot," he said.<br><br>The prescription pad came out.<br><br>"Let's start you on a daily MiraLAX. It'll be your new best friend."<br><br>The exact phrase. Twelve years late.<br><br>My hand was already reaching for the script.<br><br>My husband came with me because I'd been crying in the car for two weeks. He's a building inspector. He sat in the side chair with his hands on his knees.<br><br>He leaned forward. Quiet. The way he reads a contract before he signs it.<br><br>"Before she fills it — can someone look at what's actually broken? Her dad was on this for twelve years."<br><br>The doctor paused.<br><br>He said he could refer me to a functional-medicine specialist if I wanted. Didn't push. Pulled a card from his desk drawer and handed it to me.<br><br>I took the card.<br><br>I walked out without the prescription.<br><br>I sat in the parking lot for forty minutes before I could start the car.<br><br>I almost canceled the specialist twice.<br><br>Two hundred dollars for an intake form that asks about my father felt like grief tourism.<br><br>I drove there anyway.<br><br>Cedar Lane Functional Medicine. A converted feed-and-grain storefront at the end of Cedar Lane. Wood floors. The smell of green tea. No fluorescent lights.<br><br>The intake form was six pages. One whole page about my father.<br><br>The receptionist offered me a cup of tea. I drank it.<br><br>Dr. Nguyen came out herself to call my name. Mid-fifties. She booked one patient an hour. I was the one patient.<br><br>She didn't talk about treatment that first visit.<br><br>"Before we change anything, I want to see what's actually there."<br><br>She ordered a microbiome stool panel. Bacterial diversity. The acid-producing capacity of my gut. Inflammatory markers.<br><br>Things no one had checked in six years.<br><br>Three hundred and forty dollars out of pocket. I sent it in.<br><br>Ten days later we booked the follow-up.<br><br>She turned her monitor toward me. Color-coded bars across the screen, like a soundboard.<br><br>She pointed at the first one.<br><br>"This is your Bifidobacterium. These are the bacteria that make the chemical signal that tells your colon to contract. A woman your age should be up here."<br><br>She pointed higher. Then much lower.<br><br>"You're here. I normally see this in patients who've been on daily laxatives for years. You haven't started yet. Your bacteria collapsed from diet, stress, and aging alone."<br><br>"But my doctor said the constipation was the problem," I said.<br><br>"The constipation is the last thing to change," she said.<br><br>"Your bacteria have been declining for years. Probably more than a decade. Long before your bowel slowed."<br><br>"Every two days became three. Then four. Then five. Your doctor watched the number cross a line and reached for MiraLAX. But the collapse underneath started a decade before that number moved."<br><br>She let that sit.<br><br>"Your bowel frequency is the surface. What I'm seeing underneath it is ten years ahead of what that number tells you."<br><br>I felt sick.<br><br>"So what does the MiraLAX even do?"<br><br>She was direct.<br><br>"It pulls water into your colon by osmosis. The waste moves from pressure — not because your muscles contracted. Your doctor sees that you went and says 'working, keep taking it.'"<br><br>"But it doesn't feed the bacteria. It doesn't rebuild the signal. And every dose flushes out more of the bacteria you need."<br><br>"The output improves. The collapse underneath keeps going."<br><br>And that's when I understood what happened to my father.<br><br>Twelve years of managed output. Twelve years of bigger doses. Twelve years of his doctor saying the MiraLAX was working.<br><br>And he died of the thing they were managing.<br><br>I told her.<br><br>She was quiet.<br><br>"That's unfortunately common," she said. "The laxative managed his output for twelve years. But the bacterial collapse — the root cause — continued the whole time. His gut looked like it was working. The bacteria that send the signal were dying underneath. That's the gap the laxative can't close."<br><br>There it was.<br><br>The answer to the question I'd carried since I was 33, standing in a hospital hallway being told my father was gone.<br><br>His output was managed for twelve years. And he still died of what the laxative was supposed to prevent.<br><br>"So is the laxative my only option?" I asked.<br><br>"You have two paths," she said.<br><br>"Path one. You start the MiraLAX. The output improves. You go more often at every checkup. But the collapse keeps going underneath. The dose climbs. Magnesium gets added. Then stimulant laxatives. The output stays managed. The cause keeps dying."<br><br>She paused.<br><br>"That's the road your father was on for twelve years."<br><br>"Path two. You actually fix why your bacteria are depleted in the first place."<br><br>"How?" I asked.<br><br>"Your colon doesn't move waste on its own," she said. "It moves on a chemical signal. Organic acids your gut bacteria make."<br><br>"When the bacteria are healthy, those acids reach the receptors lining your colon. The receptors release serotonin. The serotonin is what triggers the urge, and the contraction. The waste moves through naturally."<br><br>"When the bacteria are depleted, the signal dies. The muscles just sit there. Capable. But silent. They're not broken. They're not getting the message."<br><br>She looked at me.<br><br>"That is what constipation actually is. Not a stool problem. A signaling problem."<br><br>"MiraLAX forces the output through water pressure. The number on the chart improves. But it never restores the signal. And it flushes out more bacteria every dose. Your gut becomes dependent on the bypass instead of recovering its own function."<br><br>"Your father was on that bypass for twelve years. The laxative was managing him. It wasn't healing him."<br><br>Managing. Not healing.<br><br>That's what my father was for twelve years.<br><br>"What about fiber?" I asked. "My doctor keeps saying more fiber."<br><br>"Fiber is the raw material," she said. "If the bacteria that ferment it aren't there, more fiber does almost nothing. Eighty percent of people with what you have don't respond to more fiber. That's published. That's not me being clever."<br><br>"And probiotics? I've tried those."<br><br>"Most probiotics send a few strains in that play for a week and then pass through. The category you actually need is fermentation. The finished acids, delivered daily. The way traditional cultures got them from kombucha and kefir, every day, without thinking about it."<br><br>"That is what your father never got. Your grandmother probably did, daily, without knowing why."<br><br>"Is there a way to actually restore the signal?" I asked.<br><br>"The most direct one is kombucha," she said. "It's pre-fermented. So it delivers the finished organic acids your depleted gut can't make anymore. Acetic. Lactic. Gluconic."<br><br>"Those are the same molecules that hit the receptors lining your colon and switch the serotonin signal back on."<br><br>"Then you want live cultures with chronic-constipation trial data behind them. L. plantarum and B. coagulans, to rebuild the bacteria that make the acids long-term. Inulin from dandelion root, to feed what's left of your Bifido. Slippery elm, to soothe the wall while it recovers."<br><br>"Most probiotics send a few strains that pass through. This brings the finished signal to the door."<br><br>I almost laughed.<br><br>"Fermented? My gut already ferments everything. Half of why I'm bloated."<br><br>She'd heard it before.<br><br>"That's the difference," she said. "The bloating you're describing is fermentation happening uncontrolled inside you, on food that's stuck. This is fermentation done outside the body. The acids are already finished before they ever reach you. You're not asking your gut to ferment anything. You're delivering what it can't make."<br><br>"And it's not the sugar-bomb cider gummies. Those have one acid. This is the whole matrix. Dosed daily."<br><br>She named the category. She didn't name a brand.<br><br>I went home and did my own homework.<br><br>I almost gave up before I started.<br><br>I've fallen for Align. I've fallen for Milk of Magnesia. I've fallen for twelve years of MiraLAX through my father's kitchen window.<br><br>What was a twenty-nine-dollar pouch of berry gummies going to do that thirty-dollar Align hadn't?<br><br>I almost closed the tab.<br><br>Then I thought about the scoop in my father's workshop. Worn smooth from twelve years of mornings.<br><br>The one that matched everything she'd described — pre-fermented kombucha, the finished organic acids, L. plantarum and B. coagulans, dandelion inulin, slippery elm — was Jevawell.<br><br>A resealable pouch. One raspberry gummy a day. Twenty-nine dollars. A sixty-day money-back guarantee — if it doesn't work, you send it back.<br><br>I ordered one pouch.<br><br>Then I changed the quantity to two.<br><br>One for now. One for when the first ran out.<br><br>The pouch came Thursday.<br><br>Cream-beige top. Dark green JEVAWELL across it, a little leaf in the A. Deep forest green body. A gold raspberry on the side.<br><br>I set it on the kitchen table my father built. Next to his old enamel coffee mug.<br><br>I looked at the two of them for a long minute.<br><br>Took one gummy.<br><br>Tasted berry.<br><br>Sat down.<br><br>Week one — nothing.<br><br>Week two — nothing.<br><br>I almost emailed Dr. Nguyen to ask if I should keep going.<br><br>I didn't. I kept taking the gummy.<br><br>Week three. Tuesday morning. I went, and the strain wasn't there. Twenty minutes, not ninety. The mass was softer. More complete.<br><br>I didn't tell anyone. I wasn't sure it counted.<br><br>Week five. Three movements that week. Naturally. No MiraLAX since the parking lot.<br><br>My husband noticed the bloat was down before I said a word. He reached across the table and held my hand.<br><br>Week seven. Regular. Daily. Soft. Easy. Twenty minutes a morning, not ninety.<br><br>The green dress fit again.<br><br>I tucked a shirt in for the first time in three years and wore it to work and didn't think about my stomach once.<br><br>Week twelve, Dr. Nguyen repeated the panel.<br><br>Bifidobacterium up 54 percent.<br><br>Akkermansia up 41 percent.<br><br>Faecalibacterium up 67 percent.<br><br>Still not at "normal." But moving in the right direction for the first measurable time in my adult life.<br><br>She looked at the screen, then at me.<br><br>"This is what restoration looks like," she said. "Not management."<br><br>At my own doctor's follow-up I told him I never started the MiraLAX.<br><br>He looked at the daily movements in my chart for a long moment.<br><br>"If this holds," he said, "we can leave the MiraLAX conversation where it is. Keep doing what you're doing."<br><br>It's been four and a half months now.<br><br>The orange Metamucil tubs are in the recycling.<br><br>The MiraLAX is still in the drawer, just in case. The scoop is dry. I haven't opened it since the parking lot.<br><br>The week of my father's anniversary, I had a hard stretch. Three days. The old tightness. The old dread loop.<br><br>I took one extra gummy at lunch instead of reaching for the laxative.<br><br>The body came back on its own by Wednesday.<br><br>This past Sunday morning I sat at the kitchen table my father built, with a cup of coffee.<br><br>His old enamel mug is still on the shelf where he kept it.<br><br>I drank my coffee and I went, by myself, without help. The first time in my adult life I have done that.<br><br>If you're reading this — and your drawer looks like my drawer, and your doctor sounds like my father's doctor — your constipation isn't the disease.<br><br>It's the last symptom of a collapse that started a decade before your bowel ever slowed.<br><br>My father proved where the managing road leads.<br><br>He managed output for twelve years. He still died of the thing they were managing.<br><br>I fixed the cause.<br><br>In four months my gut bacteria are healthier than they've been in a decade.<br><br>Don't wait until the managed-output road is the only road left.<br><br>Don't follow the road my father followed for twelve years.<br><br>A fermented kombucha gummy. 7;"><div style="white-space: pre-wrap;"><span>She started taking water pills at 62. Within a month, I watched her world shrink to the size of our living room.<br><br>She'd plan her entire day around her ankles. Up at 6am to get things done before the swelling started. By noon, she'd be on the couch with her feet up. By 3pm, she couldn't get her shoes back on.<br><br>She stopped saying yes to things. The book club. Dinner with friends. Our granddaughter's school play.<br><br>She'd make excuses. "I'm just tired." "It's too far." "Maybe next time."<br><br>But I knew the truth. Who carried our grandson on her hip at the zoo without thinking twice.<br><br>Gone.<br><br>Replaced by someone who shuffled from the bedroom to the couch and back again. Someone who wore long skirts in July. She's getting worse, not better. Her ankles are bigger now than they were two years ago."<br><br>He barely looked up from his screen.<br><br>"How's the fluid retention?"<br><br>"It's NOT fluid retention," I said. "It's her life. She can't do anything past noon. She can't wear her own shoes. She hasn't danced in three years."<br><br>He looked at me like I was being dramatic.<br><br>"Peripheral edema is progressive," he said. "Especially at her age. The diuretics are keeping it manageable. We need to continue the current approach."<br><br>"Manageable? My hands were shaking.<br><br>"I'm fine," she said. Quietly. Looking out the window.<br><br>She wasn't fine.<br><br>What Water Pills Actually Do (And Why Her Doctor Never Explained It)<br><br>That night, I couldn't sleep.<br><br>I sat in the spare room with my laptop and started searching. "Why do diuretics stop working." "Why does leg swelling get worse every year." "What actually causes edema."<br><br>What I found made me furious.<br><br>Diuretics work by forcing your kidneys to flush water out of your blood.<br><br>They reduce the total amount of fluid in your system. Temporarily.<br><br>That's how they reduce swelling.<br><br>But here's what Dr. Hargreaves never explained:<br><br>They don't fix WHY the fluid is leaking into her legs in the first place.<br><br>Think of it like a garden hose with holes in it.<br><br>Water is spraying out through the holes into the garden. class="_7jyh"><div><div><div class="_8nsi _8nqp _a25w"><div class="xc26acl x6s0dn4 x78zum5 x2lwn1j xeuugli" style="width: 100%;"><img alt="Better Digestion Daily" class="_8nqq img" class="xc26acl x78zum5 x2lwn1j xeuugli" style="width: 100%;"><div class="x78zum5 xdt5ytf x2lwn1j xeuugli" style="width: 100%;"><a class="xt0psk2 x1hl2dhg xt0b8zv x8t9es0 x1fvot60 xxio538 xjnfcd9 Daily</span></a><div class="_8nrv"><span class="x8t9es0 xw23nyj xo1l8bm x63nzvj x6lvj10 xq9mrsl x1h4wwuj xeuugli"><div class="_4ik4 _4ik5" style="-webkit-line-clamp: 2;"><div><span class="x14vqqas"><strong>Sponsored</strong></span><span><strong></strong></span></div></div></span></div></div></div></div></div><div class="x1plvlek xryxfnj"><div class="_7jyr _a25-"><span class="x8t9es0 xw23nyj xo1l8bm x63nzvj x108nfp6 xq9mrsl x1h4wwuj xeuugli"><div tabindex="0" role="button"><div class="_4ik4 _4ik5" style="line-height: 16px; max-height: 112px; -webkit-line-clamp: 7;"><div style="white-space: pre-wrap;"><span>There's a test that explains your constipation.<br><br>It costs a few hundred dollars. I run it for a living.<br><br>Your doctor almost certainly never ordered it.<br><br>I'm Reyna. Nineteen years on a lab bench in Mesa, Arizona. I'm the one who counts the bacteria in your gut.<br><br>And I'm not supposed to be talking to you at all.<br><br>Here's how it works where I am.<br><br>You see a doctor. They draw blood, or they hand you a kit, and somewhere on a form a box gets checked. That sample gets boxed up and shipped to a place like mine — a reference lab, the building your clinic sends things to when the test is too specialized to run in-house.<br><br>I'm the person who runs it.<br><br>I load the plate. I run the sequencer. I read the bars that come up on my screen, and I sign the report.<br><br>Then the report goes back to the doctor who ordered it. Not to you. Never to you.<br><br>Techs don't talk to patients. We don't even know your name half the time — just a number on a requisition slip. We're the back of the house. You never see us.<br><br>I'm breaking that rule today. I'll tell you why in a minute. First I need you to see what I see.<br><br>When a gut sample comes through for one of the bigger panels — the ones that actually map the bacteria living in your colon — the report has blocks.<br><br>One block is the bugs that keep things calm. One block is the troublemakers. And one block, the one I watch, is the acid-makers.<br><br>These are the bacteria that take what you eat and ferment it down into tiny organic acids. Those acids are not waste. They are a signal. They're the chemical message that tells your colon to squeeze.<br><br>On my screen they show up as bars against a line — the reference range, where a healthy gut should sit.<br><br>And here is the thing I have watched happen, over and over, for nineteen years.<br><br>On the samples that come in flagged for chronic constipation, that block is on the floor.<br><br>The acid-maker bars sit way down under the line. Sometimes barely there at all.<br><br>Meanwhile the rest of the report can look fine. The colonoscopy came back clean. The bloodwork came back clean. By every test the doctor actually ran, nothing is wrong.<br><br>But nobody ran the test that shows the bars on the floor.<br><br>Because that panel — the one that would explain the whole thing — is a send-out. Most family doctors never order it. Insurance fights it. It runs you a few hundred dollars out of pocket.<br><br>So it doesn't get ordered.<br><br>The one number your doctor does watch is how often you go. And they watch that number quietly cross a line — every four days, then every week, then longer — and when it gets bad enough, they reach into a drawer and hand you the same thing they hand everyone.<br><br>"Take MiraLAX. It'll be your new best friend."<br><br>More fiber. More water. More prunes.<br><br>And the block that would have explained all of it was never on the slip.<br><br>That's the part that started keeping me up.<br><br>I'd see the collapse on my screen at 9 a.m. and know there was a real person on the other end of that number — at home, dreading the bathroom, convinced their body was just broken — being told to eat more fiber.<br><br>And I couldn't say a word. The report goes to the doctor. Not to them.<br><br>I want to tell you about the drawer.<br><br>Not mine. The one I'd see in my head every time those bars dropped — because I'd seen the same one in my own mother's kitchen.<br><br>MiraLAX, the white powder, scooped into juice every morning.<br><br>Metamucil tubs in the back of the cabinet.<br><br>Magnesium citrate. Milk of Magnesia. Senna tablets for the desperate weeks.<br><br>Prune juice until the smell of it made her gag.<br><br>Fiber gummies that, near as anyone could tell, made the bloat worse.<br><br>A whole shelf of things that worked for exactly one week and then quit.<br><br>And I knew — from the bars on my screen — exactly why every single one of those failed.<br><br>Fiber needs those acid-making bacteria to do anything. If they're gone, the fiber just sits there. Piles up. Makes the bloat worse, not better.<br><br>MiraLAX doesn't restore the signal. It drags water into the colon to force one flush. The waste moves from pressure, not because anything contracted. Then it's over, and you're back where you started.<br><br>Probiotics? They send a couple of strains in that mostly wash right through. A capsule of two bugs can't replace the whole acid-making community that thinned out.<br><br>Every one of those is working on the surface. Not one of them touches the block on the floor.<br><br>Now I'll tell you why I'm breaking the rule.<br><br>My mother. Estela.<br><br>For years it was "more prunes, mija, drink more water." MiraLAX with her coffee. The doctor said the same things to her that the form letters say to everyone.<br><br>And I — the one who reads these panels for a living — never once thought to look at my own mother's gut.<br><br>You learn that on the bench. You don't get personal with a sample. It's a number, not a name. You keep the wall up or you can't do the work.<br><br>Then last spring she got worked up for something unrelated, and a careful internist added a stool panel onto the order. Almost as an afterthought.<br><br>It landed in my lab.<br><br>I pulled it up on my screen without even checking the name on it first. Just another run.<br><br>And there it was. The acid-maker block, flat against the floor of the range. The same collapse I'd signed off on a thousand times.<br><br>Then I saw the name on the requisition.<br><br>Salcedo, Estela.<br><br>My mother.<br><br>The data had been knowable the whole time. Sitting there. And I'd been so good at keeping the wall up that I never looked.<br><br>That was the day I stopped being just the tech.<br><br>So let me tell you what that collapsed block actually means. Plainly. The way I'd explain a result to a brand-new hire on her first week.<br><br>Your colon does not move on its own. It moves when it gets a signal.<br><br>That signal is the organic acids your gut bacteria make when they ferment your food.<br><br>The acids reach the receptors that line your colon. Those cells release serotonin. The serotonin fires the urge — and the squeeze that moves things along.<br><br>When the acid-makers thin out, fewer acids get made. The signal goes faint. The urge fades.<br><br>Your colon muscle isn't broken. It's sitting there, perfectly able, waiting for a message that isn't coming.<br><br>That's why people say they "lost the urge." That's why they say "my body forgot how to go."<br><br>It didn't forget. It went quiet.<br><br>And once I understood that, I had one question — the same one I ask about anything before I'll trust it: where's the data?<br><br>I don't take supplements on faith. I read methods sections for fun. I have thrown out plenty of things that had a nice story and no trial behind them.<br><br>So I went looking for what, if anything, actually has human evidence in chronic constipation. Not a nice idea. Not a mouse. People with the exact problem on those flagged panels.<br><br>Two things kept coming up.<br><br>A strain called Lactobacillus plantarum. And one called Bacillus coagulans.<br><br>Both have been through randomized, placebo-controlled human trials in people with chronic constipation. The people who took them had more complete bowel movements and faster transit than the people on the placebo.<br><br>Randomized. Placebo-controlled. In people. That's the standard I hold a test to, and these cleared it.<br><br>Those two strains are the slow rebuild — putting back the kind of bacteria that thinned out.<br><br>Then you have to feed them. Inulin — a prebiotic fiber from dandelion root — has its own human trials for stool frequency. The strains rebuild; the inulin feeds them. That's the foundation.<br><br>And then the part that surprised me.<br><br>Kombucha.<br><br>Not the drink. The culture.<br><br>Kombucha is already fermented. The bacteria did the work outside your body, before it ever reaches you. So it delivers the finished organic acids — acetic, lactic, gluconic — the same kind of acids your own depleted gut had stopped making enough of.<br><br>The strains and the inulin are the why-this-works — the slow rebuild underneath. The kombucha acids are the why-you-feel-it-sooner — the finished signal, handed over while the rebuild catches up.<br><br>And slippery elm, to soothe a gut wall worn raw from years of straining, while the rest recovers.<br><br>I almost laughed when I first read it.<br><br>Fermented? My mother's gut already ferments everything. Half of why she was bloated.<br><br>But that's the whole point, and it's the part I had backwards.<br><br>The bloating is fermentation happening uncontrolled, inside her, on food that's stuck. This is the opposite. The fermentation is done outside the body. The acids are finished before they ever reach you. You're not asking a worn-out gut to make the signal from scratch. You're delivering what it's been short on.<br><br>So I did what I do at work. I ignored the promises on the front and read the actual label.<br><br>I wanted those two studied strains — L. plantarum and B. coagulans, the ones with the placebo-controlled constipation trials. The dandelion inulin to feed them. The finished kombucha acids on top. The slippery elm.<br><br>The one that had all of it in a single daily dose was Jevawell.<br><br>A resealable pouch. One raspberry gummy a day. Twenty-nine dollars. A sixty-day money-back guarantee — if it does nothing, you send it back.<br><br>I almost talked myself out of it for her. I've watched a thousand drawers fail. What was a twenty-nine-dollar pouch of berry gummies going to do that thirty-dollar Align hadn't?<br><br>Then I thought about her name on that requisition slip. The bars on the floor. The years she spent being told it was prunes.<br><br>I bought her two pouches. One to start. One for when the first ran out.<br><br>I told her to take one a day and stop reaching for the laxative unless she truly had to.<br><br>Week one, nothing. Week two, nothing. She called me ready to quit. I told her to keep going — the rebuild is slow, that's not a slogan, that's what the trials actually show.<br><br>Week three. A Tuesday. She called me before eight in the morning.<br><br>She'd gone. On her own. Soft, and complete, and over in a few minutes instead of an hour of straining.<br><br>She didn't make a big deal of it. I did. I sat in the lab parking lot and cried before my shift.<br><br>Week five she was regular. Most mornings, on her own. The hard, round belly she'd carried for years had gone soft and flat. She wore a fitted blouse to church she hadn't been able to button in three years.<br><br>She sat through an entire movie last month without doing the math on where the nearest bathroom was. She told me that part like it was nothing. To her it was everything.<br><br>A few weeks in, that careful internist re-ran the stool panel.<br><br>It came across my bench again. Salcedo, Estela.<br><br>The acid-maker block had lifted up off the floor. Not all the way to normal — not yet — but up, for the first measurable time in her adult life.<br><br>I sat there looking at the bars I'd watched fail on a thousand strangers, finally moving the right direction, on my own mother.<br><br>That's not management. Management is when the surface number looks fine and the block stays on the floor. This was the block itself, moving. Her own rhythm, coming back. Supported, fed, not forced.<br><br>I have to tell you where the other road goes, because I've read those panels too.<br><br>Years ago I ran one for a woman eight years deeper into the managed-output road than my mother was. Same collapse, but worse — and her chart, by then, was about whether her colon could keep going at all, or whether the conversation turns to surgery to take part of it out. That's where the surface-managing road can end for some people, if the cause underneath keeps going unaddressed. Not the common road. But a real one. The complications, not the default.<br><br>Her acid-maker block, the whole time, had been on the floor.<br><br>Nobody had ever ordered the test that showed it.<br><br>So here's what I broke the rules to tell you.<br><br>Your constipation is probably not the disease. It's the surface — the one number your doctor watches. Underneath it, on a panel almost nobody orders, there's very often a block sitting on the floor that explains the whole thing.<br><br>You don't need the test to do something about it. My mother never had a follow-up panel until weeks in — she just fed the system back what it was short on.<br><br>The strains with the real human trials. The inulin to feed them. The finished kombucha acids on top, so you feel it sooner. One gummy. Once a day.<br><br>Your colon isn't broken. It went quiet. And a quiet gut can be fed back toward its own rhythm — that part, the data actually backs.<br><br>Your doctor is watching one number.<br><br>I spent nineteen years watching the one underneath it.<br><br>Now you can do something about it too.<br><br>It's a fermented kombucha gummy with two clinically-studied strains. One a day. 7;"><div style="white-space: pre-wrap;"><span>I am a colorectal surgeon. I have performed seventy-one colectomies in twelve years on women who could not stop straining.<br><br>For twelve years I have been the woman who could not stop straining.<br><br>A nurse on my own floor caught me in the stairwell on a Tuesday and asked me a question that ended the lie.<br><br>I want to tell you the question.<br><br>And I want to tell you why a surgeon who removes colons for a living had not, in twelve years, fixed her own.<br><br>Let me start with why I do this work.<br><br>My mother was constipated her whole life.<br><br>Nobody ever figured out why.<br><br>By the time she was sixty-four it had a name, and by the time she was sixty-eight she had a partial colectomy.<br><br>She never got her life back after that.<br><br>So I went into colorectal surgery.<br><br>I trained at the best program in the country.<br><br>I learned to take out a sigmoid colon better than almost anyone in this state.<br><br>And the entire time I was learning to do that, my own gut was getting worse.<br><br>I started straining in college.<br><br>By residency I was chewing magnesium every day.<br><br>By the time I finished my fellowship I was going to the bathroom once every nine days.<br><br>Once every eleven when I traveled for conferences.<br><br>I never told a single attending.<br><br>Not one.<br><br>You learn, in surgery, to keep your hands steady and your face still.<br><br>I kept my whole life still.<br><br>I wore scrubs, and scrubs hide everything.<br><br>Eighteen months ago, after a colonoscopy showed slow transit, I did something quietly.<br><br>I ordered a stool-bacteria panel on myself, under a different name.<br><br>The bacteria that are supposed to make the chemical signals my colon needs to move?<br><br>Nearly gone.<br><br>I read the result.<br><br>I filed it in a drawer.<br><br>And I kept operating.<br><br>I want you to understand what that means.<br><br>I was standing over women, removing the parts of their colon that had stopped working, while carrying the same condition in my own body, with the same result on a piece of paper I had hidden.<br><br>Now the Tuesday.<br><br>It was between my second and third case.<br><br>There is a stairwell in the surgical wing, Stairwell B, that has no foot traffic between nine and eleven in the morning.<br><br>I knew that the way you know things you are ashamed of.<br><br>I had chewed three magnesium tablets in the lounge an hour earlier.<br><br>I was hunched over the railing, one hand white-knuckled on the steel, sweating, trying to get my body to do the one thing it would not do, before I had to scrub in and ask another body to hold still under my hands.<br><br>The door above me opened.<br><br>It was Denise.<br><br>Fifty-one. A paralegal.<br><br>One of my own patients.<br><br>Three weeks earlier she had been on my schedule for a consult, and there was a colectomy referral with her name on it sitting on my desk.<br><br>She stopped on the landing.<br><br>She looked at me bent over that railing.<br><br>And she said, very quietly:<br><br>"You've been doing this too, haven't you."<br><br>It was not a question.<br><br>She had recognized her own posture in my body.<br><br>I have been cut open, figuratively, in a lot of rooms in my life.<br><br>That stairwell was the one that opened me all the way.<br><br>Because here is the thing about the shame.<br><br>The shame was the proof.<br><br>If a colorectal surgeon who had read every paper in this field had this exact problem — and could not fix it with everything she knew — then the problem was not "lazy bowels."<br><br>It was not "she didn't drink enough water."<br><br>It was not willpower.<br><br>It was something underneath all of that.<br><br>Something my entire training had never taught me to look for.<br><br>I took Denise to the surgical lounge after my third case.<br><br>I pulled up my own panel on the lounge computer.<br><br>The one I had hidden for eighteen months.<br><br>I turned the screen toward her.<br><br>And for the first time, out loud, I told another person the truth.<br><br>I am going to tell you the same thing I told her.<br><br>In plain language.<br><br>The way I wish someone had told me in the first year of residency.<br><br>Your colon does not move on its own schedule.<br><br>It moves when it gets a chemical signal.<br><br>That signal is made by specific bacteria living in your gut.<br><br>They take what you eat and ferment it into a small family of molecules called short-chain fatty acids.<br><br>Three of them matter most.<br><br>Acetate.<br><br>Propionate.<br><br>Butyrate.<br><br>Those molecules land on a receptor on the cells lining your colon.<br><br>The receptor is called FFAR-2.<br><br>When that receptor is switched on, it turns on the enzyme that makes serotonin in your gut.<br><br>Gut serotonin is what tells the colon to contract.<br><br>That is the whole chain.<br><br>Bacteria, then acids, then the receptor, then serotonin, then the squeeze that moves everything along.<br><br>When the chain works, you go to the bathroom without thinking about it.<br><br>When the bacteria that make those acids are gone, the acids stop being made.<br><br>When the acids stop being made, the receptor goes quiet.<br><br>When the receptor goes quiet, the serotonin is not released.<br><br>When the serotonin is not released, the colon does not contract.<br><br>The signal does not fire.<br><br>My colon was not sick.<br><br>It was unsignaled.<br><br>I want you to hold that sentence the way I have held it every day since.<br><br>Your colon didn't break. It stopped getting the signal.<br><br>Sitting in that lounge, I finally understood the things that had never made sense to me.<br><br>I understood why fiber had only ever made me more bloated.<br><br>Fiber assumes there are bacteria home to ferment it.<br><br>There weren't.<br><br>Not in me.<br><br>And not in most of the women I had cut.<br><br>I understood why magnesium worked the day I took it and never fixed anything underneath.<br><br>Magnesium forces water in.<br><br>It does not make a single signal molecule.<br><br>And I knew, as a surgeon, that years of leaning on it can weaken the very muscle I was counting on.<br><br>I understood why MiraLAX moved me once and never gave me a morning back.<br><br>It is water in the colon.<br><br>It is not a signal.<br><br>And then I understood the worst one.<br><br>The colectomy.<br><br>The operation I had built my career on.<br><br>It removes the part of the colon that has stopped getting the signal.<br><br>It does not restore the signal.<br><br>I looked at Denise and I said the truest thing I have ever said to a patient.<br><br>"The reason your referral has been sitting on my desk for three weeks is that I cannot tell you to do something I knew — the day I read your tests — would not give you back your bowel."<br><br>I want to say something carefully here, because I do not want to be melodramatic about it, and I do not believe in melodrama.<br><br>I do not believe the medical system is hiding anything from you.<br><br>The history of fermented food and gut function is sitting in the public literature.<br><br>The 2024 human trial on kombucha and these exact signal-producing bacteria is free to read.<br><br>The reason none of it was ever taught to me — by professors I respected, by attendings I owe my whole career to — is not a conspiracy.<br><br>It is structural.<br><br>You cannot patent a fermented food.<br><br>You cannot patent a live bacterial signal.<br><br>There is no twenty-million-dollar trial pipeline behind something a Korean family has been making in clay pots for centuries.<br><br>The training I received was paid for by the molecules that can be patented.<br><br>And those molecules do not restore the signal.<br><br>They move output past a starved signal.<br><br>That is the gap.<br><br>That is the gap I performed seventy-one surgeries inside of.<br><br>I am writing this so I do not perform a seventy-second.<br><br>So that afternoon, in front of Denise, I did something I had never done in twelve years.<br><br>I took her colectomy referral off the stack on my desk.<br><br>And I tore it up.<br><br>I want to be clear about what that means and what it does not mean, because I am still a surgeon and I will not pretend otherwise.<br><br>Denise's referral was an elective one, for He died at 64 of complications from chronic constipation.<br><br>Three months ago I sat in the same exam-room chair he sat in and my doctor reached for the same prescription.<br><br>I almost said yes — until my husband asked one question that would have saved my father's life.<br><br>I'm 44.<br><br>My father has been gone for nine years now. The spring our youngest started kindergarten.<br><br>The death certificate said "complications from chronic constipation, sepsis pathway." I didn't even understand what that meant until I read the discharge summary on the plane home from the funeral.<br><br>He was a quiet man. A bridge engineer for the state DOT for thirty-six years. He measured things for a living.<br><br>The MiraLAX showed up on his kitchen counter the year I turned 30.<br><br>His GP said the line I've thought about every week since.<br><br>"This is your new best friend now."<br><br>That exact phrase.<br><br>My father wrote it down on a Post-it inside the kitchen cabinet. I found it cleaning out the house. New best friend. In his engineer's handwriting.<br><br>For twelve years he scooped the white powder into his orange juice every morning at 6:15 AM. I watched him do it from my teenage kitchen, and then later from the kitchen I came home to visit.<br><br>He'd say "I'm regular as a clock."<br><br>He'd say it like a small joke at family dinners. Like a man reporting from a bridge inspection.<br><br>I believed him.<br><br>The year before he died, he started saying his belly felt "tight." He was 63. The GP said keep up the MiraLAX, maybe try a little Metamucil with it.<br><br>He did.<br><br>The week he died I didn't know how bad it had gotten. The hospital said sepsis. The hospital said impaction. The hospital used the word "perforation" and I asked them to please not use the word "perforation" with my mother in the room.<br><br>Twelve years of managed output.<br><br>He died of the thing they were managing.<br><br>I started slipping around the time my fortieth birthday came and went.<br><br>Every other day. Then every third. Then every fourth.<br><br>By 42 it was every four to five days at best.<br><br>The bloat showed up at 8 PM like a guest who would not leave. I stopped wearing my wrap dress because I look six months pregnant by dinner. Stopped tucking shirts in. Started pulling sweaters around my waist in every photo.<br><br>I dread thinking about when I will poop.<br><br>I stopped saying that out loud somewhere around my 40th birthday because I could hear my mother saying it about my father.<br><br>The strain hour at 6 AM, the door locked, my knees pulled up to my chest, my eyes closed for ninety minutes while the rest of the house slept.<br><br>Pebble stools when I did go. Rabbit pellets. Blood on the paper one morning — I cried in the bathroom and then I went to work.<br><br>The drawer.<br><br>I stood in front of it one night and I made myself list it out loud.<br><br>MiraLAX. White powder, the orange juice in the morning.<br><br>Metamucil. Three orange tubs stacked in the back.<br><br>Magnesium citrate. The green-and-yellow soda bottle I'd chug on Sunday nights. Tastes like grapefruit lighter fluid.<br><br>Magnesium glycinate. The calmer one. Didn't really move anything.<br><br>Senna. The brown tablets. The whip I'd take when I had a flight Tuesday.<br><br>Dulcolax suppositories. The box in the back. The emergency drawer.<br><br>Milk of Magnesia. Four months of chalky nightly chugs. Bloated belly that wouldn't quit. Stopped working after three rounds.<br><br>Castor oil. Three days. The smell. Three hours of cramping for ten minutes of release. Never again.<br><br>Probiotics. We fell for Align. Thirty a month for six months. Three good weeks. Then nothing.<br><br>Smooth Move tea. The kettle on at 9 PM every Sunday.<br><br>Prune juice. Every morning until I gagged at the sight of the bottle.<br><br>Triphala. Two weeks of working, then nothing.<br><br>Fiber gummies. Two different brands. Made the bloat worse.<br><br>The squatty potty under the bathroom sink.<br><br>The colonoscopy at 41. Nothing remarkable.<br><br>A pelvic-floor PT referral I canceled twice and never went to.<br><br>I closed the drawer.<br><br>Stood there in the dark.<br><br>Half of those were in my father's cabinet too. I'd been buying them my whole life and not seeing it.<br><br>This past New Year's I drove down to help my mother sort my father's old papers.<br><br>We sat at the same kitchen table I grew up at.<br><br>In the back of the cabinet behind the coffee mugs, I found an unopened MiraLAX packet.<br><br>I held it.<br><br>Sat down with it in my hand.<br><br>Set it on the counter next to my coffee.<br><br>Drove home that night.<br><br>Booked the first available appointment with my new GP — my old one had retired the year before — and made a note in my phone to actually go this time.<br><br>Three weeks later I was sitting in Exam Room 4 of the same medical-park complex my father had used for fifteen years.<br><br>I didn't realize that until I walked in and saw the framed lithograph of a covered bridge on the wall.<br><br>Same lithograph my father used to make fun of. A bridge engineer making fun of a bridge lithograph for fifteen years.<br><br>The chair.<br><br>The vinyl exam chair with the cracked armrest.<br><br>The same chair.<br><br>I sat down in it and I could feel my father sitting in it.<br><br>My husband came with me because I had been crying in the car for two weeks. He sat in the side chair with his hands on his knees.<br><br>The doctor was kind. He was thorough. He listened for six minutes.<br><br>Then he said "you've tried a lot."<br><br>Pulled out the prescription pad.<br><br>"Let's start you on a daily MiraLAX. It'll be your new best friend."<br><br>The exact phrase.<br><br>Twelve years late.<br><br>I almost said yes. My hand was already reaching for the script.<br><br>My husband leaned forward in the side chair.<br><br>Quiet. Not aggressive. The way he asks the auto mechanic things.<br><br>"Before she fills it — can someone look at what's actually broken? Her dad was on this for twelve years."<br><br>The doctor paused.<br><br>Said he could refer me to a functional-medicine specialist if I wanted. Didn't push. Pulled a card out of his desk drawer and handed it to me.<br><br>Dr. Aurelia Marchetti. Foundation Functional Medicine. Cottage office on Maple Street.<br><br>I took the card.<br><br>Walked out without the prescription.<br><br>Sat in the parking lot for forty minutes before I could start the car.<br><br>I almost canceled the appointment with Dr. Aurelia twice.<br><br>Two hundred dollars for an intake form that asks me about my father felt like grief tourism.<br><br>I drove there anyway.<br><br>A converted craftsman cottage at the end of Maple Street. Wood floors. A window seat with a wool throw on it. The smell of bergamot tea coming out of what used to be a dining room.<br><br>The receptionist offered me a cup. I drank it.<br><br>Dr. Aurelia came out herself to call my name. Not a medical assistant. Mid-fifties, gray bob, reading glasses on a beaded chain.<br><br>She booked one patient per hour. I was the one patient.<br><br>The intake form was six pages. One whole page about my father.<br><br>She didn't talk about treatment that first visit. She said: "Before we change anything, I want to see what's actually there."<br><br>Ordered a microbiome stool panel.<br><br>Three hundred and forty dollars out of pocket.<br><br>I almost didn't send it in.<br><br>I sent it in.<br><br>Ten days later the results came back and we booked a follow-up.<br><br>Second appointment.<br><br>She turned her monitor toward me. Pulled up the chart. Color-coded bars across a screen that looked like a soundboard.<br><br>"Your bowel frequency — every four to five days — is the surface. The damage underneath is ten years worse than that number suggests."<br><br>She let that sit.<br><br>Then she said the thing I wrote down in my phone notes app in the parking lot afterward.<br><br>"The laxative is like repainting a house with a crumbling foundation. The walls look fine from the street. The beams are rotting underneath."<br><br>She paused.<br><br>"Your father's beams rotted for twelve years while his doctor was repainting."<br><br>I started crying in the chair. She handed me a tissue from a wooden box and waited.<br><br>Then she walked me through the panel.<br><br>She pointed to the first bar.<br><br>"Bifidobacterium. These should be in the top three populations in a healthy colon. Yours is in the bottom ten percent. These are the bacteria that ferment fiber into the chemical signals that tell your colon to contract."<br><br>Second bar.<br><br>"Akkermansia muciniphila. Should be at three to five percent. Yours is at zero point four. These bacteria maintain the mucus layer that protects the wall of your gut. When they're gone, the wall thins. Constipation accelerates the loss, because stool sits there longer and dries the mucus out."<br><br>She looked up from the screen.<br><br>"Every day on MiraLAX is a day the Akkermansia don't come back."<br><br>Third bar.<br><br>"Faecalibacterium prausnitzii. Should be five to ten percent. Yours is at zero point eight. These produce butyrate. Butyrate is the single most important short-chain fatty acid for the health of your colon wall and the signal that tells the muscles to contract."<br><br>She turned the screen back toward herself.<br><br>"Short-chain fatty acids — acetate, butyrate, propionate — are the chemical signals your bacteria send to the muscles of your colon. Without those signals, the muscles sit in their chairs. They are not broken. They are not getting the message."<br><br>I said, "But my GP said more fiber —"<br><br>She cut in. Gently.<br><br>"Fiber is the raw material. If the bacteria that ferment it aren't there, more fiber is more concrete you can't pour because there's no mixer. Eighty percent of people with what you have don't respond to more fiber. That's published. That's not me being clever."<br><br>I started to say something about probiotics and she got there first.<br><br>"Most probiotics send one violinist to an empty stage. They show up in your gut, play for a week, and pass through. The category you actually need is fermentation. Pre-finished postbiotics. Delivered daily. The way traditional cultures got them from kombucha, kefir, fermented vegetables, every day, without thinking about it."<br><br>She tapped the screen.<br><br>"That is what your father never got. Your grandmother probably did, every day, without knowing why."<br><br>Then she said the thing about MiraLAX.<br><br>"MiraLAX is polyethylene glycol. It pulls water into the colon. That's all it does. It doesn't feed the bacteria. It doesn't restore the signal. It manages output. It doesn't heal anything."<br><br>She looked at me for a long moment.<br><br>"It is repainting. Twelve years of repainting is what we saw on your father's death certificate."<br><br>I sat in the chair and looked at the wool throw on the window seat across the room.<br><br>She let me sit there.<br><br>Then she said — and this is the line I wrote down too —<br><br>"You are not your father. You're sitting here. He didn't get this conversation. You are."<br><br>Near the end of the hour she mentioned, almost in passing, that there was one fermented postbiotic supplement she'd been recommending to her chronic-constipation patients for about a year.<br><br>A kombucha-derived gummy.<br><br>She wrote the name on a Post-it.<br><br>Jevawell.<br><br>A pre-fermented kombucha culture — the postbiotic matrix that delivers the organic acids my bacteria stopped making. Acetic. Lactic. Gluconic. The same molecules that activate the colon receptors my missing bacteria normally would have. Plus two probiotic strains with chronic-constipation trial data — L. plantarum and B. coagulans — to start rebuilding the populations that ferment the acids long-term. Inulin from dandelion root to feed what was left of my Bifido. Slippery elm to soothe the gut wall while the rebuild happens.<br><br>"I have no financial relationship with them," she said. "I just keep seeing my patients come back regular for the first time in a decade. You can search it."<br><br>She handed me the Post-it.<br><br>I put it in my wallet between the credit cards.<br><br>I drove home with the Post-it in my wallet and the microbiome chart on my phone.<br><br>I didn't go to the kitchen.<br><br>I went to my father's old desk in the spare room. The one my mother gave me when she sold the house.<br><br>Opened the bottom drawer.<br><br>Pulled out a manila folder of my father's last year of doctor's notes. I had kept them and never read them.<br><br>I read them at the desk at 10:30 PM with my husband asleep upstairs.<br><br>Twelve years of "increase MiraLAX dose."<br><br>Twelve years of "patient reports tightness, recommend stay the course."<br><br>Zero microbiome panels.<br><br>Zero discussion of bacteria.<br><br>Zero discussion of postbiotics.<br><br>I closed the folder. Sat with it on my lap.<br><br>He didn't know. His doctor didn't know.<br><br>I do know. I have the panel. I have the Post-it.<br><br>I pulled out my phone.<br><br>Typed in Jevawell.<br><br>Read the page. Kombucha culture, slippery elm bark, dandelion root, soluble fiber, the two probiotic strains. A prebiotic-probiotic-postbiotic stack. Sixty-day money-back guarantee.<br><br>Then I almost closed the tab.<br><br>I've fallen for Align. I've fallen for Milk of Magnesia. I've fallen for castor oil. I've fallen for twelve years of MiraLAX through my father's kitchen window.<br><br>What was a twenty-nine-dollar pouch of berry gummies going to do that thirty-dollar bottles of Align hadn't?<br><br>I almost closed the tab.<br><br>Then I pulled the Post-it out of my wallet.<br><br>Looked at Dr. Aurelia's handwriting.<br><br>I went back to the page and I ordered one pouch.<br><br>Then I changed the quantity to two.<br><br>One for now. One for when the first ran out.<br><br>The pouch arrived Thursday. Tracking said four days.<br><br>Cream-beige top panel. Dark green JEVAWELL wordmark with a little leaf in the A. Deep forest green body. Gold raspberry-and-leaves on the side.<br><br>I set it on the kitchen counter next to my father's old coffee scoop.<br><br>Looked at the two of them for a long minute.<br><br>Took one gummy.<br><br>Tasted berry.<br><br>Sat down at the kitchen table.<br><br>Week one — nothing.<br><br>Week two — nothing.<br><br>I almost emailed Dr. Aurelia to ask if I should keep going.<br><br>I didn't.<br><br>I kept taking the gummy.<br><br>Week three — Tuesday morning. I went, and the strain wasn't there. Twenty minutes, not ninety. The mass was softer. The movement was more complete.<br><br>I didn't tell anyone. I wasn't sure it counted.<br><br>Week five — three movements that week. Naturally. No MiraLAX since the parking-lot afternoon. No senna in the morning.<br><br>I told my husband over coffee on Saturday. He didn't say anything. He reached across the table and held my hand.<br><br>Week seven — regular daily. Soft. Easy. Twenty minutes a morning, not ninety.<br><br>The wrap dress fit again.<br><br>Week twelve — Dr. Aurelia repeated the panel.<br><br>Bifidobacterium up 54%.<br><br>Akkermansia up 41%.<br><br>Faecalibacterium up 67%.<br><br>Still not at "normal." Three days, the old tightness, the old dread loop. I took one more gummy at lunch instead of reaching for the laxative.<br><br>The body came back on its own by Wednesday.<br><br>The foundation is the foundation.<br><br>The weather still moves over it.<br><br>This past Sunday morning I sat at my parents' old kitchen table with a cup of coffee.<br><br>My mother makes the coffee in my father's old pot. class="x14vqqas"><strong>Sponsored</strong></span><span><strong></strong></span></div></div></span></div></div></div></div></div><div class="x1plvlek xryxfnj"><div class="_7jyr"><span class="x8t9es0 xw23nyj xo1l8bm x63nzvj x108nfp6 xq9mrsl x1h4wwuj xeuugli"><div tabindex="0" role="button"><div class="_4ik4 _4ik5" style="line-height: 16px; max-height: 112px; -webkit-line-clamp: 7;"><div style="white-space: pre-wrap;"><span>My father took MiraLAX every morning for twelve years. He died at 64 of complications from chronic constipation.<br><br>Earlier this year I sat in the same exam-room chair he sat in and my doctor recommended the same white powder.<br><br>I almost said yes — until my husband asked the one question no one ever asked my father.<br><br>Every test my father ever took came back normal.<br><br>He died of the thing they were managing.<br><br>I'm 51. I'm not a doctor. I'm not selling anything. I'm the daughter of a man who scooped white powder into orange juice every morning for twelve years, and I need to tell you what I found out too late to tell him.<br><br>My father was a bridge engineer for the state DOT for thirty-six years. Quiet man. Measured things for a living.<br><br>The MiraLAX showed up on his kitchen counter the year I turned 30. His GP had a phrase for it.<br><br>"This is your new best friend now."<br><br>My father wrote it down on a Post-it inside the kitchen cabinet. His engineer's block letters. NEW BEST FRIEND. Underlined once.<br><br>I found it years later cleaning out the house. It's the one thing of his I kept.<br><br>For twelve years he scooped white powder into orange juice at 6:15 in the morning. Same scoop. Same glass. "Regular as a clock," he'd say. Like a small joke. Like a man reporting in from a bridge inspection.<br><br>I believed him.<br><br>The year before he died, his belly started feeling tight. He was 63. The GP said keep up the MiraLAX. Maybe add a little Metamucil.<br><br>He did. He did exactly what they told him.<br><br>The week he died, he didn't tell my mother how bad it had gotten. He didn't tell me.<br><br>The death certificate said complications from chronic constipation, sepsis pathway. On the flight home from the funeral I made myself read the discharge summary, word by word, until I understood it.<br><br>A stool impaction had blocked his bowel. It sat there long enough that the wall tore. The infection went into his blood.<br><br>He was 64.<br><br>My father measured bridges for a living, and he died on a bathroom floor of constipation.<br><br>I know how that sounds. I didn't believe it either, until I read it in a hospital's own words.<br><br>Twelve years of managed output.<br><br>Every test he ever took came back normal.<br><br>He died of the thing they were managing.<br><br>I want to tell you what happened to me before I tell you what I found out. Because if you're a woman around my age reading this, some of it is going to sound like the inside of your own house.<br><br>It started for me a few years after he was gone. I was 45, maybe 46.<br><br>Every other day. Then every third. Then every fourth. By 48 it was every four or five days at best.<br><br>And somewhere in there the urge itself went quiet.<br><br>I don't know how to describe that to someone who hasn't lived it. I used to at least feel it coming. By 48 I felt nothing. No signal. No warning. Like my body had forgotten how to go on its own.<br><br>I only went when I made myself go.<br><br>The bloat showed up at 8 PM like a guest who wouldn't leave. I stopped wearing the wrap dress because I looked six months pregnant by dinner. Stopped tucking shirts in. In every photo from those years I'm pulling a sweater around my waist.<br><br>The strain hour at 6 AM. Door locked. Knees pulled up to my chest. Sixty minutes with my eyes closed while the rest of the house slept.<br><br>Pebble stools when I did go. Rabbit pellets. One morning there was blood on the paper and I cried in the bathroom for two minutes and then I went to work.<br><br>I dread thinking about when I will poop.<br><br>I stopped saying that out loud around the time it got bad. I could hear my mother saying it about my father.<br><br>The drawer.<br><br>I stood in front of it one night, in the dark, and made myself list it out loud like naming the dead.<br><br>MiraLAX.<br><br>Metamucil.<br><br>Magnesium citrate.<br><br>Magnesium glycinate.<br><br>Senna.<br><br>Dulcolax suppositories.<br><br>Milk of Magnesia.<br><br>Castor oil.<br><br>Align.<br><br>Smooth Move tea.<br><br>Prune juice.<br><br>Triphala.<br><br>Fiber gummies. Two brands.<br><br>The squatty potty under the sink.<br><br>A colonoscopy at 41. Nothing remarkable.<br><br>A pelvic-floor referral I canceled twice and never went to.<br><br>I closed the drawer.<br><br>Stood there.<br><br>Half of those were in my father's cabinet too. I'd been buying them my whole life and not seeing it.<br><br>And one night it landed on me. I have two kids. Someday one of them is going to clean out my kitchen.<br><br>I did not want them finding my Post-it.<br><br>This past January, around the anniversary of his death, I drove down to help my mother sort my father's old papers.<br><br>We sat at the kitchen table I grew up at.<br><br>In the back of the cabinet, behind the coffee mugs, I found an unopened MiraLAX packet. His. Nine years old.<br><br>I held it. And I understood I was standing exactly where he'd stood.<br><br>I drove home that night and booked an appointment with a new GP — my old one had retired the year before. I wasn't going for a refill. I wanted someone to look at me and tell me I wasn't turning into my father.<br><br>I made a note in my phone: actually go this time.<br><br>Three weeks later I was sitting in Exam Room 4 of the same medical-park complex my father had used for fifteen years.<br><br>I didn't realize it at first. Then I saw the framed lithograph of a covered bridge on the wall.<br><br>The same lithograph my father used to make fun of. A bridge engineer, making fun of a bridge lithograph, for fifteen years.<br><br>The chair.<br><br>The vinyl exam chair with the cracked armrest.<br><br>The same chair.<br><br>I sat down in it and I could feel my father sitting in it.<br><br>My husband came with me because I'd been crying in the car for two weeks. He sat in the side chair with his hands on his knees.<br><br>The doctor was kind. He was thorough. He listened for six minutes.<br><br>Then he pulled a notepad over and started writing it down for me.<br><br>"Pick up a tub of MiraLAX on your way home. Daily. It'll be your new best friend."<br><br>The same seven words. A different doctor said them to my father in a different room in this same building, twelve years before.<br><br>And my hand was already moving toward that pad.<br><br>I want you to understand that. After the flight home. After the discharge summary. After nine years. My hand was reaching for the same powder that killed him.<br><br>That is how strong the pull is.<br><br>That is how they get you.<br><br>My husband leaned forward in the side chair. Quiet. Not aggressive. The way he asks the mechanic about the car.<br><br>"Before she starts that — can somebody actually find out why this keeps happening? Her dad was on that stuff for twelve years."<br><br>The doctor paused.<br><br>Said he could refer me to a functional-medicine doctor if I wanted. Didn't push. Pulled a card out of a drawer and handed it to me.<br><br>Dr. Aurelia Marchetti. Foundation Functional Medicine. On Maple Street.<br><br>I took the card. Walked out without starting anything.<br><br>Then sat in the parking lot for forty minutes before I could turn the key.<br><br>I almost canceled the appointment with Dr. Aurelia twice. Two hundred dollars for an intake form that asks about my father felt like grief tourism.<br><br>I drove there anyway.<br><br>A converted craftsman cottage at the end of Maple Street. Wood floors. A window seat with a wool throw on it. Used to be somebody's dining room. Smelled like bergamot tea.<br><br>The receptionist offered me a cup. I drank it.<br><br>Dr. Aurelia came out herself. Not an assistant. Mid-fifties, gray bob, reading glasses on a beaded chain. She books one patient an hour. I was the patient.<br><br>The intake form was six pages. One whole page about my father.<br><br>She read all of it before she said a word. Then she read my colonoscopy from 41, the bloodwork, the years of nothing remarkable.<br><br>She put it down.<br><br>"I'm not going to send you for another scan. You've had them. They're normal."<br><br>I started to say that was the whole problem. That everything was always normal.<br><br>She nodded before I finished.<br><br>"That's the cruel part of this. What's actually wrong doesn't show up on any of them. It didn't show up on your father's either."<br><br>Then she said something I did not see coming.<br><br>She took her glasses off.<br><br>"I want to tell you something before we go any further. I spent twenty years of my practice sending people home for that same powder your father was on. 'This is your new best friend.' I said those words too. To a lot of women who looked like you."<br><br>"I sent them home with the powder and I told them we would monitor it."<br><br>She set the glasses on the desk.<br><br>"I did not understand what I was actually doing until I started looking at what the drug never touched. It took me a long time. I'm sorry it took me a long time. Your father's doctor was doing what he was trained to do. So was I."<br><br>She let that sit.<br><br>"I'm telling you this because I want you to know I know how that room felt today. I sat in a lot of those rooms."<br><br>She had a little notepad. She drew a slow line across it.<br><br>"A few times a day, your colon is supposed to squeeze. Hard. One strong contraction that sweeps everything down and out. That squeeze is what you feel as the urge. It's run by a little band of cells in the wall of the colon. Pacemaker cells. Same idea as the ones that keep a heart on beat."<br><br>She tapped the line.<br><br>"In someone like you, those cells have been wearing down. For years."<br><br>I asked her how she could possibly know that. If no scan shows it.<br><br>"Because I've watched it walk through that door a hundred times. Women exactly like you. Every test clean. A little worse every year. And when researchers look at colons like that under a microscope, the cells that fire the squeeze are worn down. What wears them down is oxidation."<br><br>I asked her what that meant.<br><br>She reached over and picked up an apple from a small dish beside her desk.<br><br>"Let me show you."<br><br>She cut it in half with a paring knife. Set one half on a small plate between us, cut side up. Left it there.<br><br>"Watch it while we talk."<br><br>She kept going.<br><br>"Deep in the wall of your colon, right against the layer where the muscle sits, are these pacemaker cells. Nobody's told you about them because you weren't supposed to know about them. When they work, you don't think about it. You just go."<br><br>She glanced at the apple.<br><br>"They are being damaged. Worn down. By free radicals your own gut has been overproducing for years. Processed food. Stress. A round of antibiotics here and there. All the ordinary things. They wipe out the good bacteria and leave the lining raw. And a raw lining throws off far too many of these corrosive little molecules. Day and night. They don't switch off."<br><br>She paused.<br><br>"The cells barely grow back. So the damage stacks up. Year after year. The squeeze gets weaker. Then it comes less often. Then it stops coming on its own at all."<br><br>Then she said the line.<br><br>"And one day, you notice the urge is just gone."<br><br>The urge. The thing I'd stopped feeling at 48.<br><br>She nodded down at the plate. The cut side of the apple had gone soft brown while she talked.<br><br>"Nothing touched it. That's oxidation. Free radicals — the same molecules — breaking the flesh down from the inside."<br><br>She picked up a wedge of lemon from the dish and squeezed half of it over a fresh slice. Set it on the plate next to the brown one.<br><br>"Watch this one. It won't turn. That's what an antioxidant does. It steps in and neutralizes the free radicals before they can do the damage."<br><br>She set the knife down.<br><br>"It's the same chemistry that rusts a steel beam. It has been oxidizing the cells in the wall of your colon that fire the contraction. You can't see it on any scan — which is why every test came back normal while you got worse."<br><br>Then, quiet.<br><br>"Your cells have never once gotten the lemon juice."<br><br>She let that sit.<br><br>"In my read, that's what's happening. Nobody can put a scan on it and prove it to you. Not yet. But it is the best explanation we have for why you are doing everything right and still getting worse."<br><br>She looked at me.<br><br>"It isn't your willpower. It isn't your fault. It's the modern gut, not you. The cells aren't dead. Take away what's corroding them and give the contraction a chance to come back."<br><br>"You are not broken. You did not forget how. The cells that run it have been wearing down. Quietly. The whole time your tests were coming back normal."<br><br>She let that sit too.<br><br>"That is why your father's came back normal. For twelve years."<br><br>I put my hand over my mouth.<br><br>Nine years. A death certificate. A discharge summary I made myself read on a plane. And the thing that killed him had been sitting there under every clean test the whole time, and no one ever went looking for it.<br><br>She handed me a tissue from a wooden box on her desk and waited.<br><br>I said, "But they kept telling him more fiber. They told me more fiber too."<br><br>"Fiber is a raw ingredient. Your bacteria are supposed to ferment it. But the same diet that started this wiped those bacteria out. So the fiber just sits there and turns to gas. That's why it made you more bloated, not less."<br><br>She shrugged.<br><br>"You can't out-eat a contraction that isn't firing."<br><br>I started to say something about the laxatives.<br><br>She got there first.<br><br>"A stimulant laxative — your senna, your Dulcolax — doesn't fix anything. It lashes the muscle into one forced squeeze. That isn't your body doing the work. That's your body being whipped into it. It works once. Then it quits. Then it needs a bigger dose."<br><br>She looked at me.<br><br>"Your father proved his colon could be forced for twelve years. He never once got to find out if it could work on its own."<br><br>I couldn't answer that.<br><br>"And the MiraLAX," she said, "pulls water in so what's already sitting there slides out. You go, a little. Wet, full, and still no real urge — because the squeeze still isn't happening. It clears out today. It does nothing about why the squeeze stopped coming."<br><br>She capped her pen.<br><br>"You can't fix a contraction that isn't firing by softening or bulking what it's supposed to move. You have to go after what is damaging the cells that fire it."<br><br>I looked at the wool throw on the window seat across the room and I didn't say anything for a while.<br><br>She let me sit.<br><br>Then she said the thing I typed into my phone in the parking lot afterward, the one I've read a hundred times since.<br><br>"You are not your father. You're sitting here. He never got this conversation. You are."<br><br>Near the end of the hour I asked her the only question left. So what do I actually do.<br><br>She uncapped the pen again.<br><br>"That's the hard part. It isn't one job. To fix this, you have to do three things at the same time."<br><br>She wrote them down the side of the page.<br><br>"One. Stop the damage. That is an antioxidant's job — neutralize those free radicals so they quit wearing the cells down.<br><br>Two. Calm the gut that's making them. Soothe that raw lining and put back the good bacteria the modern diet stripped out.<br><br>Three. Get the contraction some help while you rebuild. Two strains with their own trials in people with what you have. One for going more often. One for getting through faster."<br><br>She turned the page toward me.<br><br>"Everything in that drawer of yours worked on what happens downstream. Not one of them stopped the damage, calmed the source, and helped the squeeze come back. All three, at once."<br><br>She said it plainly.<br><br>"The treatments failed you. You did not fail."<br><br>Ten years I had been calling myself broken. A woman I'd met forty minutes earlier was the first person to say out loud that it wasn't me.<br><br>I asked her what does all three.<br><br>"Stopping the damage is the antioxidant. And the strongest one I keep coming back to for these cells — the one that actually gets to the free radicals doing the damage — is kombucha."<br><br>She nodded at the plate between us. The slice that was still white.<br><br>"The lemon juice."<br><br>I must have made a face.<br><br>She smiled.<br><br>"Not the drink. The drink is the worst version of it. Heat kills the antioxidant. Every shelf-stable bottle has been heated. Every so-called live bottle is still fermenting in your fridge — making more alcohol and gas, not more of what you need. doing in three months.<br><br>I do not say this to be poetic. What matters is the signal isn't there."<br><br>I asked the question every woman in my position asks.<br><br>"But I eat eighteen grams of fiber at breakfast."<br><br>He nodded. Adding more fiber to a colon that can't ferment it is what has been making the bloating worse. Not better. We have to put the bacteria back first."<br><br>I asked the second question every woman in my position asks.<br><br>"What about Miralax."<br><br>He breathed out a little.<br><br>"Miralax pulls water into the bowel. The longer you use it, the further you get from your own body's rhythm. After enough years, your colon forgets it is supposed to know how to do this on its own."<br><br>I felt Don's hand find mine.<br><br>I felt the cold linoleum under my feet.<br><br>I asked the third question. The one I had not known I was going to ask.<br><br>"What if we do nothing."<br><br>He didn't answer right away.<br><br>He looked at the stills on the monitor. That was somehow worse than if he had said it with drama.<br><br>He said it like a man who has had this conversation two hundred times.<br><br>He set the pen down.<br><br>"The dilation will not reverse," he said. Slippery elm is the soothing layer."<br><br>He underlined the third.<br><br>"Dandelion root feeds the few good bacteria you still have. Specifically the butyrate producers. The Tuesday in October the first really cold front came through.<br><br>The discharge summary said "complications from chronic constipation." I had to look it up on my phone in the hospital parking lot. The funeral was on a Saturday. I gave the eulogy without crying. I cried in the car afterward, alone.<br><br>She was a quiet woman. An elementary-school teacher for thirty-four years. First graders. Same district. Retired at 62.<br><br>Her lesson plans sat in a binder by the door, dividers labeled in her neat cursive. Mon. Tue. The laminator stayed on the kitchen table every Sunday afternoon, the smell of warm plastic underneath the smell of coffee.<br><br>She could say one sentence — "eyes up here, friend" — and a room of six-year-olds would go quiet.<br><br>She kept thirty first-graders regular as recess. Her doctor kept forcing the flush.
