7;"><div style="white-space: pre-wrap;"><span>I tore something at 2 a.m. last Tuesday on my own bathroom floor, eighteen days after the last time my body let me go, and I have not told a single living person until right now.<br><br>I'm 58 years old.<br><br>I can fix any furnace in Marion County in the dark.<br><br>And for the better part of a year I could not make my own body do the one thing every healthy person does without thinking about it.<br><br>I'm going to tell you what a man named Hutch said to me on a folding chair at a gun-and-knife show last month. It's the reason I'm not still carrying a plastic syringe in my coat pocket.<br><br>And I think somebody else reading this is carrying one too.<br><br>My name is Dale. I fix heating and cooling in Marion, Ohio, and have for almost forty years. I have fixed furnaces that other guys condemned.<br><br>I could not fix me.<br><br>Let me back up to that Tuesday night.<br><br>It was 2 in the morning. I couldn't sleep for the pressure. Eighteen days since my body had let me go, and my belly was hard and round and tight — press on it and it doesn't give back.<br><br>I was on the bathroom floor with a heating pad and a small plastic syringe of warm water. That's the part I'm most ashamed of.<br><br>Months back I found a forum where men like me wrote about it. You fill a small plastic syringe with warm water and flush out what's stuck, low down, so you can get enough out to feel safe leaving the house. That's what I was doing at 2 a.m. — so I could go do a furnace call the next day without carrying a brick around inside me.<br><br>And halfway through, a fissure I'd had for weeks tore again.<br><br>If you've had it, you know the words. The ring of fire. The blood when you wipe. The thing that happens every single time now.<br><br>I sat back against the tub, and I thought: I am a 58-year-old man kneeling on my own bathroom floor at 2 in the morning with a syringe, and I can't tell Linda, and I can't tell anybody.<br><br>I didn't feel like a human being. Somewhere along the way I'd stopped feeling like one.<br><br>That was the bottom.<br><br>Now let me tell you how I got there, because it didn't happen overnight.<br><br>It started maybe a year before that night, quiet. I just… stopped getting the feeling.<br><br>The whole signal to go quit firing. It wasn't that I was straining and nothing came. There was nothing there to strain toward. No urge at all. My body had stopped telling me.<br><br>At first it was once a week and I figured, fine, I'm getting older. Then once every nine days. Then closer to two weeks. The number kept creeping the wrong way and I kept not saying anything.<br><br>My belly was hard by every afternoon. My waistband got two notches looser and I was still bloated.<br><br>Here's the part nobody tells you. On a backed-up day, eating more just made it worse. You're piling food onto a system that's already stuck — that full, heavy, almost-sick feeling with nowhere to go. So I started skipping lunch on jobs. I dreaded eating. Me. A man who used to love a diner breakfast.<br><br>I'd wake at 3 a.m. with trapped gas. I lived on magnesium so long it fogged my head and dragged my mood into a hole.<br><br>And the whole time, I had a story for it. I blamed it on getting older. On thirty years of gas-station food in the truck. On my back. On sitting too much. I had not been blaming it on one thing I could actually fix.<br><br>By the end I'd quit hoping. This was just who I am now. A guy whose body forgot how to work.<br><br>I just wanted to poop like a normal person. Not a miracle. Just the thing everybody else gets for free.<br><br>And I'd tried everything.<br><br>There's a drawer in our bathroom vanity. Linda calls it my drawer. MiraLAX — every morning with my coffee, religiously. Metamucil. Magnesium citrate. Magnesium glycinate. Senokot. Dulcolax. Milk of Magnesia. Smooth Move tea. Psyllium. Prune juice. Align — thirty dollars a month. Culturelle.<br><br>A whole drawer of stuff that worked for exactly one week and then quit.<br><br>And I drank the water — eight, ten glasses a day. I ate the fiber. I walked. I'd done everything every doctor ever told me.<br><br>I went to my GP, Dr. Easton, more than once across two years.<br><br>First visit: "More fiber. More water. Try Metamucil." I almost laughed. I had a drawer of it. Next visit, down to once every nine days: "MiraLAX is going to be your new best friend." It was already my best friend.<br><br>By the last visit I was closer to two weeks. He ran a sleep apnea test for the brain fog, it came back negative, and he said, "A lot of men your age, Dale. Let's keep an eye on it."<br><br>The number kept creeping — nine days, fourteen, eighteen — while the whole system kept an eye on it.<br><br>Here's what I was really scared of, underneath all of it.<br><br>My brother-in-law, Marv — Linda's older brother, 64 — is the man who taught me this trade. Same lifelong broken plumbing. Same drawer of failures. Same "just eat more fiber" from every doctor for thirty years. Same survival hack — he's done his own flushes for years.<br><br>And last fall his gastroenterologist sat him down and said the words I cannot get out of my head: when the flushing finally quits on him, the next step is cutting the colon out and hanging a bag off his side for good.<br><br>That's it. That's the end of the line. The colon gone, a bag for the rest of his life.<br><br>Marv keeps the appointment card on his fridge. I see it every time we're over there.<br><br>That's the road I knew I was on. Marv was just further down it.<br><br>So that brings me to the swap meet.<br><br>There's a gun-and-knife show at the county fairgrounds most months. I almost didn't go that Saturday because my gut was bad, but Linda told me to get out of the house.<br><br>I was sitting stiff in my folding chair behind a table of old tools, pale, not talking to anybody, when the man at the next table slid a coffee across to me. His name was Hutch. Short for Hutchins. Around 66. Big, slow, easy man.<br><br>He looked at me and said, "You don't have to tell me what's wrong. But I know that look. Sit a minute."<br><br>I found out later why he knew it. Hutch spent thirty years as an orderly at the VA hospital — wheeling people to and from colorectal surgery. He'd seen a thousand men with the look on my face.<br><br>And something in the plain way he said it cracked me open. I told him everything. The eighteen days. The syringe. The floor at 2 a.m. The tearing. It was the first honest thing I'd done in eight months. He didn't flinch. He'd wheeled men far worse.<br><br>Then he said, "Can I tell you something? Don't take it as advice. Take it as a story."<br><br>And he told me about his late brother, Earl.<br><br>Earl went down the exact road Marv is on. Years of flushing. Then the flushing stopped working. Then the surgery. Then the bag. And Earl, Hutch said, was never the same man again.<br><br>I thought about Marv's appointment card on the fridge, and the floor dropped out from under me.<br><br>But then Hutch did something nobody had done in eight months. He told me that what was wrong with me had been done TO my body. It wasn't something wrong WITH me.<br><br>After a year of every doctor making it sound like a character flaw — try harder, drink more, eat more fiber — here was a man telling me my body had a cause, not a defect. For the first time, I let myself believe I wasn't as fundamentally broken as I thought I was.<br><br>Because Earl's daughter — a hospice nurse — had found something one layer deeper than every doctor had looked.<br><br>Hutch wrote a name on the back of a flyer and put it in my hand.<br><br>I drove home careful, and that night Linda and I sat at the kitchen table and read everything we could find. Here's the whole thing the way I finally understood it. Stay with me, it's plain.<br><br>The colon doesn't move on its own. It moves when it gets a signal — an actual chemical signal made by the bacteria living in your gut.<br><br>When those bacteria ferment what you eat, they release tiny organic acids. And those acids are what tell the colon to contract.<br><br>That contraction is the urge. That feeling I'd lost? That's it. A signal.<br><br>And here's what happened to me. Years of antibiotics, stress, and the standard American diet wiped out the bacteria that make the signal.<br><br>No bacteria. No acids. No signal. No urge. That's why I'd lost the feeling.<br><br>My body wasn't broken. It had gone silent.<br><br>And once I understood that, everything in my drawer made sense.<br><br>Fiber needs those bacteria to do anything. If they're gone, it just sits there and piles onto the stuck system — which is why it made me more bloated, not less. MiraLAX doesn't bring the signal back; it drags water in to force one flush, then it's over. 7;"><div style="white-space: pre-wrap;"><span>For twenty years I prepped people for the surgery where they cut out part of your colon.<br><br>Last spring a doctor looked at my own chart and told me I was three years from that same conversation.<br><br>And I had done everything right.<br><br>Eight glasses of water. The fiber. The MiraLAX every morning with my coffee, religiously.<br><br>I'm the nurse who hands you the bowel prep the night before your scope.<br><br>I'm the one who sits with you when the doctor says the words "we should talk about taking part of it out."<br><br>I've done that job for two decades.<br><br>I never once thought I'd be the one in the paper gown.<br><br>Let me tell you how it happens. Because it doesn't happen the way you think.<br><br>It doesn't happen to the people who ignore their doctors.<br><br>The cases that scared me most were never the ones who skipped the appointments or ate junk or never moved.<br><br>They were the careful ones.<br><br>The women who drank the water. The same ladder, every time.<br><br>MiraLAX first. Then Metamucil. Then magnesium. Then senna when the magnesium quit. Then a specialist. Then the conversation about the surgery.<br><br>I handed people that ladder for twenty years and I believed in it. I'd even smile and say it the way you're supposed to. "This one's going to be your new best friend."<br><br>Then my own body started climbing it.<br><br>At first I blamed the job.<br><br>Twelve hours on my feet. Skipped lunches. Getting older. That's what I told myself.<br><br>But the full ritual stopped working.<br><br>I was going maybe once every two weeks. Even with the water. Even with the fiber. Even with the daily MiraLAX.<br><br>And the mornings I did go never felt finished.<br><br>By 3 in the afternoon my scrub waistband cut a red welt into my side.<br><br>By evening I looked six months pregnant. Counting the stalls. Knowing which one was free.<br><br>That was the day I admitted I'd become a patient.<br><br>So I scheduled my own colonoscopy. The exact one I'd prepped a thousand strangers for.<br><br>I knew the room. I knew the cold gel. I knew the doctor.<br><br>I was still in the paper gown when he sat down with my chart.<br><br>And he said the line.<br><br>The line I have heard him say to patients for twenty years.<br><br>The line I have said myself, in those words, a hundred times.<br><br>"If the laxatives stop working, we start talking about taking part of it out."<br><br>A sluggish colon. Maybe less.<br><br>I knew exactly what that sentence meant because I'd watched it come true for so many people.<br><br>For the first time it was pointed at my own body.<br><br>I want to tell you what I did next. Because I almost did the normal thing.<br><br>He wrote me a new prescription. A stronger laxative. The next rung up the ladder.<br><br>And I sat there holding it.<br><br>And something in me refused.<br><br>Because that prescription was the same one in the chart of every patient I'd ever prepped for that surgery.<br><br>Their laxatives were doing their job. She runs the hospital's gut-health clinic, down the hall from my endoscopy suite.<br><br>A dietitian. The one I'd referred patients to for years.<br><br>A door I walked past every single shift for twenty years.<br><br>I had never once gone in as a patient.<br><br>That afternoon I knocked.<br><br>I asked her the one question I had never asked in two decades on the floor.<br><br>"Then what actually helps it work again? If the laxatives don't, what does?"<br><br>She pulled out a chair.<br><br>"Sit down," she said. "Because you've been asking the wrong question for twenty years. So has everybody."<br><br>Here is what she told me.<br><br>"Your colon doesn't move on willpower," she said. "It doesn't move on water either. It moves when the bacteria in your gut send it a chemical signal. The signal is made of short-chain fatty acids — tiny molecules your gut bacteria produce. They hit a receptor in your colon wall, the cells there release serotonin, and that's the urge. No signal, no urge. Simple as that."<br><br>She called it the signal. That's the word she used the whole time, so that's the word I'll use.<br><br>Then she glanced at the MiraLAX I'd just admitted I took every morning.<br><br>"Years of this," she said, "and the laxative does the moving for you. So the bacteria that make the signal never have to. It manages the surface. It moves the stool. The magnesium you've been leaning on before long shifts manages the surface too. None of it rebuilds the thing that stopped working. So the things you've been taking to go don't teach your body how to go on its own."<br><br>I'd handed that exact ladder to patients for twenty years.<br><br>I felt sick.<br><br>"What about fiber?" You're not doing it wrong. There's nothing there to act on it."<br><br>Everything I had said to patients, gently, with a clipboard in my hand, came back to me.<br><br>More water. More fiber. Recommend Metamucil and exercise.<br><br>Patient returns. Says the urge is gone completely. Doctor's notes: functional. Likely stress-related.<br><br>Patient returns. Down to one movement every two weeks. Doctor's notes: discuss long-term management.<br><br>Five visits. Five years. Five separate diagnoses. Five separate prescriptions.<br><br>Then someone finally sends the case to me.<br><br>I run the transit study. Read the tracing. And in less than an hour I find what explains every single one of those visits.<br><br>Silence.<br><br>The colon's pacemaker cells — the ones that fire the contraction that moves you — barely sparking. The slow waves that should ripple down the gut, flat.<br><br>The serotonin trigger that fires the urge, missing. Not blocked. Missing. There was nothing left to send the message.<br><br>And underneath all of it, the reason: the bacteria that make the chemical signal — the short-chain fatty acids that tell the colon to squeeze — gone. Starved out years ago.<br><br>Five years of doctors. Five prescriptions. Thousands of dollars. And the answer was sitting on my readout in under an hour.<br><br>—<br><br>This is what I see every single day. It never changes. The symptoms are always the same. The wrong diagnoses are always the same. The years of suffering are always the same.<br><br>And the silence is always there. The signal gone. The urge waiting for a message that never comes.<br><br>So when I got invited to present at a gastroenterology conference in Seoul last spring, I added two extra weeks to the trip. Because something had been bothering me for years. Something I couldn't explain with anything I'd learned in 12 years of studying these patients.<br><br>Korea has one of the highest rates of daily fermented-food consumption in the developed world. Cultured vegetables eaten at breakfast. Doenjang stirred into the morning soup. Kimchi aged for months and eaten with every meal of the day.<br><br>In my field, the standard line is that motility declines with age. Everyone slows down. That's first-year textbook material. Every researcher knows it. We treat constipation in the elderly like gravity — inevitable, just part of getting old.<br><br>But the rural elders outside Seoul have one of the most reliable, regular guts in the developed world. In the villages, in the communities that haven't changed their food habits in a hundred years, you find people in their 90s who go every single morning like clockwork, with no laxatives, no fiber pills, no straining.<br><br>That makes no sense. Based on my training, a 90-year-old gut should be the slowest, most stalled gut in the room. They should have MORE of what I see in my patients every day. Not less.<br><br>I needed to understand why.<br><br>—<br><br>After the conference I took a train out of Seoul into the countryside. Rolling farmland. Mountains. Villages where every household keeps its own clay crocks buried by the back door.<br><br>I arranged a homestay through a university contact who had spent years doing fieldwork in the region.<br><br>The woman I stayed with was named Soon-ja. She's 94 years old. Lives alone in the house she was born in. Tends her garden. Walks to her neighbor's farm twice a week. Cooks everything herself.<br><br>And every single morning she eats food she fermented herself — cabbage and radish that sat in those buried crocks for months. Cultured. Sour. Alive. Exactly the way her mother made it. She sets a bowl of it on the table at breakfast that she pulled from the crock the day before.<br><br>My researcher brain is going haywire sitting at her kitchen table on day two. I'm looking at this old woman eating breakfast and mentally cataloguing every patient her age who's down to one movement a fortnight. By every chart I've ever read, her gut should be a stalled, silent pipe.<br><br>This woman has been eating fermented food every single day of her life. Based on everything I know, her motility should be long gone.<br><br>But she's 94. Her eyes are sharp and quick. She has a flat stomach. She stood at her stove for two hours that morning making soup without sitting down once.<br><br>I had to ask.<br><br>"Soon-ja, at your age — do you ever have trouble? Going?"<br><br>She stops. Sets down her spoon. Looks at me the way a grandmother looks at a child who has just asked something both intelligent and deeply naive.<br><br>"Never. Not one day in my life. And it is exactly the thing you city people threw away that keeps me going."<br><br>—<br><br>She wipes her hands and tells me to sit down properly.<br><br>"You want to know why the old women in this village never strain? Why my neighbor still goes every morning at 99? Why I have buried three doctors who told me my insides would slow down with age?"<br><br>"It's because we feed the gut what it actually eats. Every single day. Since we were girls. Our mothers would not let us leave the table without it."<br><br>"City people swallow a pill to push the stool out. But the pill does nothing for the part that's broken. It forces the door open and walks away. The thing that tells the gut to move — you cannot buy that in a pharmacy. You have to feed it back."<br><br>She shakes her head.<br><br>"Our grandmothers understood this. You cannot wake up a gut by pushing from the bottom. You must feed the signal from the top. With food that is already alive."<br><br>I sat there staring at her. I have a PhD in gut physiology. I have 12 years of laboratory research. I've published papers on colonic signaling and motility failure.<br><br>And this 94-year-old woman just described the exact limitation of every laxative on the market that I've been documenting in my research for over a decade. In one sentence. Like it was obvious.<br><br>—<br><br>She gets up and goes to a shelf near the stove. Comes back with a small dark jar, the glaze worn soft from decades of use.<br><br>"Every morning before anything else, I eat a spoon of this. The water from the crock. The sour part. The part most people throw out." She sets it on the table. "It is the most alive thing in my kitchen. And I sleep, and I wake, and my body knows what to do."<br><br>"My mother gave me my first crock when I married. She ate from hers every morning of her life. She lived to 99. Her mother before her. Every woman in this village who lives past 90 does the same thing. We don't talk about it with strangers. But among ourselves everyone knows."<br><br>"The sour water goes in. Deep into the gut. Where the pills only push past. It carries the message back. And the gut remembers how to move on its own."<br><br>She presses her hand gently against her stomach.<br><br>"In the morning is when the gut wants to wake. That is when you must feed it. If you wait until it has gone silent, the medicine only forces it. It never teaches it again."<br><br>Then she said something that stopped me completely.<br><br>"Your doctors give you a pill to push the stool out. They never once ask why your gut stopped pushing on its own."<br><br>—<br><br>I need you to understand what it felt like to hear that.<br><br>I am the scientist who studies this. I have the readouts. I have the data. I have 12 years of published research.<br><br>And this woman, with no degree, no lab, no microscope, just described four things I know to be scientifically true:<br><br>One. The gut moves on a chemical signal. She said the gut has to be told to move. She's right. The colon doesn't run on muscle alone — it contracts when serotonin fires the urge, and serotonin only fires when short-chain fatty acids hit the right receptors on the gut wall. No signal, no urge. That's the whole disease.<br><br>Two. The signal comes from fermentation. She said you feed it with food that is already alive. That's exactly what the science supports. The bacteria that make those fatty-acid signals get starved out by years of Western eating, antibiotics, and stress. Fermented food brings the finished acids back — already made, ready to fire the receptor.<br><br>Three. Laxatives never restore the signal. She said the pill forces the door and walks away. She's right. MiraLAX pulls water. Senna whips the muscle. Neither one rebuilds the bacteria or the signal. The moment you stop, the silence comes back — worse, because now the muscle is weaker too.<br><br>Four. The morning timing matters. She said you feed the gut when it wants to wake. She's right. The colon's strongest natural push comes in the first hour after waking. Feed the signal then and you work with the body's own clock instead of overriding it at night.<br><br>Four facts. Twelve years and a PhD to confirm them. She learned them from her mother.<br><br>—<br><br>I spent the rest of that week talking to everyone I could.<br><br>Soon-ja's neighbor is 99. Eats from her crock every morning. Has since she was a girl. Told me her mother would check that she'd eaten her spoonful before letting her run off to the fields.<br><br>The woman two houses down is 91. Same practice. Passed to her from her grandmother. "It's not medicine," she told me. "It's just how you eat. Like washing your face."<br><br>An elder from the village, a man of 89 who still tends his own garden, told me: "We eat what is alive because it keeps the inside moving. The young people eat from boxes now. That is why they are bound up. Always has been."<br><br>I looked at these people the way I look at my readouts. Flat stomachs. Clear eyes. Steady. No bloating. No straining. No drawer of laxatives by the bed.<br><br>Then I think about my patients. People in their 40s and 50s. Bloated. Exhausted. One movement every two weeks. Being told it's IBS. Being told it's fiber. Being told it's just age. Years of antibiotics, stress, and processed food starve out the bacteria that produce them. Fiber can't fix that — fiber is the raw material those dead bacteria were supposed to ferment. You can't ferment with bacteria that are gone.<br><br>That's the limitation I've been documenting for 12 years. Every fiber pill, every probiotic capsule fails for the same reason.<br><br>But Soon-ja wasn't swallowing fiber and hoping. 7;"><div style="white-space: pre-wrap;"><span>My mother took MiraLAX every morning for fifteen years.<br><br>She died at 67 of sepsis from a bowel impaction nobody saw coming.<br><br>Last month my doctor handed me the same prescription and I almost filled it.<br><br>The paper sat on my kitchen counter for nine days. Next to my keys. Folded once down the middle. I walked past it every morning on my way to the coffee pot and pretended I wasn't seeing it.<br><br>I'm 49. I live alone. There is no one else in this house to ask me what the prescription is for or why I haven't filled it.<br><br>That part matters.<br><br>My mother was a quiet woman.<br><br>She worked thirty-one years at the same regional bank. She wore the same gold cross around her neck every day of her adult life. She made coffee at 5:45 in the morning, before her shift, in the same blue mug with the chipped handle.<br><br>I was twenty-eight the first time I saw the white powder go into her cup.<br><br>"My doctor said this is my new best friend now."<br><br>That was the phrase. Verbatim. She said it the way you say something you've decided not to question.<br><br>She used MiraLAX in her coffee — not orange juice, she didn't like sweet things in the morning — every day for fifteen years.<br><br>I visited every other Sunday. I watched her scoop the powder from the kitchen table. After a few years I stopped looking at it. After a few more, I stopped asking.<br><br>"I'm regular as a clock," she'd say.<br><br>She said it like a small reassurance. The way you tell a child a story is over and they don't have to worry anymore.<br><br>The last three years of her life she started saying her belly felt "full all the time."<br><br>She was sixty-five.<br><br>Her GP added Metamucil to the MiraLAX. He didn't run a single panel. He said "at your age, this is what we manage."<br><br>The week she died I was at a work conference in Charlotte. I hadn't called Sunday.<br><br>She went to the ER on Tuesday feeling tight. They admitted her Wednesday. By Thursday morning she was on a ventilator. She died Friday afternoon.<br><br>The discharge summary said: sepsis secondary to fecal impaction with bowel wall compromise.<br><br>I had to look up what "fecal impaction" meant on my phone, standing in the hospital parking lot, in the August heat.<br><br>That was two summers ago. The August it didn't rain once.<br><br>My own constipation started around the time I turned forty-two.<br><br>Subtle at first. Every other day became every third. Every third became every fifth. By forty-five I was going every five or six days at best.<br><br>By forty-seven I had stopped saying it out loud, to anyone, including myself.<br><br>You learn to live around it.<br><br>You learn which skirts not to wear because by six in the evening you look six months pregnant. You learn which side of the closet to push toward. You buy three long cardigans on a Saturday and tell yourself you just like cardigans now.<br><br>You sit on the toilet for an hour with your knees pulled up and your eyes closed and your phone face-down on the floor. You learn to listen for your downstairs neighbor's TV through the floor so the silence doesn't feel quite so loud.<br><br>You pass rabbit-pellet stools.<br><br>You see blood on the paper on a Tuesday and you go to work anyway.<br><br>You stop telling your friends. You stop telling your sister. You stop telling your GP after the third visit because each time he said "more fiber, more water, more walking" and you wanted to put your head on his desk and cry.<br><br>You start dreading meals because eating is just the front end of the same long question — when will I poop?<br><br>You stop having a body that feels like yours.<br><br>And every time you describe one of these things to yourself, even silently, in your own kitchen, alone, you see a flash of your mother doing the same thing.<br><br>Her hand on her lower belly at nine PM watching the news.<br><br>The gold cross flat on a swollen stomach.<br><br>The blue mug. The white powder.<br><br>I'm fine.<br><br>She said I'm fine for fifteen years.<br><br>I'm saying it now to no one, because no one is in the room to ask.<br><br>I had a drawer.<br><br>After my mother died, six months later, the following February, I drove to her apartment to clean it out. I'd put it off twice. My ex-husband would've helped me three years before that. He wasn't around for this one.<br><br>I went alone.<br><br>I emptied the kitchen. The bedroom. The hall closet. The little desk by the window where she paid her bills with a pen that had her name engraved on it.<br><br>Then I opened the bathroom cabinet.<br><br>Three unopened MiraLAX packets on the top shelf.<br><br>Half a bottle of magnesium citrate.<br><br>A blister pack of Dulcolax.<br><br>A box of senna tablets.<br><br>A jar of prune juice in the fridge two feet away, cream and white label, three quarters full.<br><br>I stood there with my hand on the cabinet door for a long time.<br><br>Because that cabinet was my cabinet.<br><br>Item for item.<br><br>I had built it for seven years without seeing it.<br><br>I closed the door. Sat on the edge of the tub. Drove home that night with her gold cross in my pocket because I couldn't make myself wear it. Booked an appointment with my own GP the next morning.<br><br>This is what was in my drawer, that February, on the morning I sat on my bathroom floor with the door open and counted.<br><br>MiraLAX — the white powder, my doctor's "new best friend."<br><br>Metamucil — two orange tubs stacked.<br><br>Magnesium citrate — the green-and-yellow soda bottle. Tastes like grapefruit lighter fluid. I chugged it Sunday nights.<br><br>Magnesium glycinate — the calmer one. Made me sleepy. Didn't move anything.<br><br>Senna tablets — the brown ones. "The whip," I called them. For Mondays before a Tuesday flight.<br><br>Dulcolax suppositories — the box in the back. The emergency drawer.<br><br>Milk of Magnesia — four months of chalky nightly chugs. Huge bloated belly. Stopped working after three rounds.<br><br>Castor oil — three days. The smell. Three hours of cramping for ten minutes of release. Gave up.<br><br>Align — I fell for Align. Thirty a month for five months. Two good weeks, then nothing.<br><br>Smooth Move tea — the kettle on at nine PM every Sunday.<br><br>Prune juice — every morning until I gagged at the sight of the bottle.<br><br>Triphala — three weeks of working, then nothing.<br><br>Fiber gummies — two brands. Made the bloat worse.<br><br>A squatty potty under the sink.<br><br>A colonoscopy at forty-three. "Nothing remarkable. Mild slow transit, common at your age."<br><br>A pelvic-floor PT referral I canceled twice and never went to.<br><br>Six sessions with an acupuncturist because a coworker swore by it.<br><br>I sat there on the tile and I thought: Item for item.<br><br>My cabinet is my mother's cabinet.<br><br>I have been becoming her in this bathroom for seven years and no one was here to see it.<br><br>I went to my GP the week of the first frost. Last month.<br><br>He's been my GP for four years. Same practice as my mother's old doctor. New office building. Same wallpaper, almost.<br><br>He listened for eight minutes.<br><br>He said, "You've tried a lot. Let's just put you on a daily MiraLAX. It'll be your new best friend."<br><br>The exact phrase.<br><br>I drove home with the prescription in my purse. Put it on the kitchen counter next to my keys.<br><br>I didn't fill it that day.<br><br>I didn't fill it the next day.<br><br>I didn't fill it the day after.<br><br>It sat there for nine days.<br><br>On the ninth night I poured a glass of wine after work and walked into the kitchen.<br><br>I stood at the counter and looked at the folded paper.<br><br>Then I walked into the bathroom and opened the drawer.<br><br>Then I walked back into the kitchen and opened my phone.<br><br>I searched: why did my mother die of constipation.<br><br>I read for two hours.<br><br>I learned what fecal impaction does to a colon wall over fifteen years. I learned about bacterial dysbiosis. I learned the word butyrate. A hospice-adjacent integrative medicine clinic in a single-story brick building with a wheelchair ramp.<br><br>I'd driven past it. I remembered thinking it looked like a yoga studio.<br><br>I called them at eight the next morning before I let myself talk myself out of it. The intake was two hundred and sixty dollars. Before we look at any of the numbers."<br><br>She leaned forward.<br><br>"For fifteen years, what we did with your mother — what we did with everyone in your mother's generation — was re-shingle the roof every year while the beams rotted underneath. From the street, the house looked fine. The shingles were clean. The shutters were painted. The output was managed."<br><br>"But the beams — the bacterial signaling architecture that holds the whole structure up — those beams collapsed quietly for fifteen years. By the time the ceiling caved in, no one knew where to look."<br><br>I wrote that down. On a napkin. Yours is in the bottom fifteen percent. These are the bacteria that ferment fiber into the chemical signals that tell your colon muscles when to contract. Without them, the muscles are getting no signal."<br><br>She pointed at the second.<br><br>"Akkermansia muciniphila. Should be at three to five percent. Yours is at zero point three. These are the bacteria that maintain the mucus layer that lines and protects your gut wall. When they're gone, the wall thins. Stool sits there longer. The mucus dries out. Every day on a laxative without restoring the Akkermansia is a day the wall keeps thinning."<br><br>She pointed at the third.<br><br>"Faecalibacterium prausnitzii. Should be five to ten percent. Yours is at zero point six. These produce butyrate. The most important short-chain fatty acid for colon-wall health and motility signaling."<br><br>She set the pen down.<br><br>"Short-chain fatty acids — butyrate, acetate, propionate — are the chemical signals the bacteria send the colon muscles to tell them when to contract. Your mother's muscles weren't broken. They just weren't getting the signal. For fifteen years."<br><br>I said, "My GP told me more fiber —"<br><br>She interrupted me. Kindly.<br><br>"Fiber is the raw material. If the bacteria that ferment it aren't there, more fiber is more lumber stacked on a foundation that can't hold it. About eighty percent of people with what you have don't respond to more fiber. That's published. That's not me being clever."<br><br>She kept going.<br><br>"And before you ask about probiotics. Most probiotics deliver one or two strains that show up, play for a week, and pass through. Like one violinist on an empty stage. What you actually need is fermentation. The pre-finished postbiotic byproducts the bacteria make — delivered daily, the way your grandmother got them from kombucha, kefir, fermented vegetables, sauerkraut. That is a different category. That is what your mother never got. Your grandmother probably did, daily, without ever knowing why."<br><br>Then she said the line about MiraLAX.<br><br>"MiraLAX is polyethylene glycol. An osmotic agent. It pulls water into the colon. It does not feed bacteria. It does not restore the architecture. It does not lay one new beam. It is re-shingling. Fifteen years of re-shingling is what we saw in your mother's discharge summary."<br><br>She paused.<br><br>She looked at me directly.<br><br>"You are not your mother. You're sitting here. She didn't get this conversation. You are."<br><br>I wrote that down too. In my phone notes, in the parking lot afterward, sitting in my car with the engine off.<br><br>Near the end of the hour she mentioned, almost as an aside, that there was one fermented postbiotic supplement she had been recommending to her chronic-constipation patients for about a year.<br><br>A kombucha-derived gummy.<br><br>A pre-fermented kombucha culture — the postbiotic matrix that delivers the organic acids my mother's bacteria had stopped making. Acetic. Lactic. Gluconic. The same molecules that activate the colon receptors her missing bacteria normally would have. Plus two probiotic strains with chronic-constipation trial data — L. plantarum and B. coagulans — to start rebuilding the populations that ferment the acids long-term. Inulin from dandelion to feed what was left of the Bifido. Slippery elm bark to soothe the gut wall while the rebuild happens.<br><br>She wrote the name on the back of her appointment card.<br><br>Jevawell.<br><br>"I don't have a financial relationship with them," she said. You can look it up."<br><br>She handed me the card.<br><br>I held it the whole drive home.<br><br>I almost didn't order it.<br><br>That night, after dinner, I sat at my kitchen table and pulled up the website on my laptop. I have fallen for fifteen years of MiraLAX in my mother's coffee cup. I am about to type my credit card number into a website at ten PM, alone, because a stranger in a linen blazer made me cry.<br><br>I almost closed the tab.<br><br>Then I looked at the appointment card on the table.<br><br>Naomi's handwriting. Black ballpoint pen. We need to go now."<br><br>I helped her up.<br><br>I got her into the car in her sweatshirt and pajama pants.<br><br>I told the girls we were going to the hospital and to text us if they needed anything.<br><br>I started driving.<br><br>—<br><br>In the car, in the dark, on the twenty-three minute drive to the ER on the south side of town, my wife told me everything she had been hiding for nine months.<br><br>—<br><br>She told me about the Miralax.<br><br>She told me about the magnesium citrate.<br><br>She told me about the fiber gummies — three brands, none of which worked.<br><br>She told me about the Squatty Potty I had wondered about.<br><br>She told me about the prune juice.<br><br>She told me about the Smooth Move tea that was making her cramp at three in the morning.<br><br>She told me about the hot lemon water at five in the morning.<br><br>She told me about the low-FODMAP diet she had been on for six weeks without telling me, which is why she had stopped eating my mother's lasagna at the Sunday dinner in September.<br><br>She told me she had been buying Miralax at the Walgreens by her work because she did not want me to see the boxes adding up at the CVS by our house.<br><br>She told me she had been crying on the bathroom floor most nights for eight months.<br><br>—<br><br>I did not say anything for the longest stretch of road.<br><br>I just drove.<br><br>Then I said the only thing I could think to say, which was: "Why did you not tell me."<br><br>She said: "I tried, Joe. The first month I tried."<br><br>I do not remember her trying.<br><br>She might have tried.<br><br>I might have been watching basketball.<br><br>I do not know anymore. I just know that nine months had passed and I had not asked her once how her body was doing while she was on a medication that was changing her body.<br><br>—<br><br>We pulled up to the ER at 11:34 PM.<br><br>I dropped her at the entrance. She insisted on walking in herself. She walked in bent over with one hand on her stomach.<br><br>I parked. I went in.<br><br>She had already been triaged. She was on a gurney behind a curtain in the third bay, an IV in her left arm, a saline drip going.<br><br>The on-call doctor was a woman in her fifties named Dr. Erin Calderon. She had short grey hair and the kind of glasses you wear after thirty years of reading charts.<br><br>She took one look at the chart and one look at me and she said, quietly, in the hallway: "Can I talk to you for a minute outside the bay."<br><br>—<br><br>I followed her around the corner to a small consult room with a sink and a poster about hand-washing.<br><br>She closed the door behind us.<br><br>She said: "Your wife is the third GLP-1 patient I have admitted with this exact pattern this week."<br><br>She said it like she was angry. Not at us. At someone else.<br><br>She said: "We are going to give her a soft cleanout, IV fluids, an X-ray to make sure there is no impaction. She will be okay tonight. She will go home tomorrow morning. But I want to talk to you about what is actually happening here, because if you do not understand it, she is going to be back in this bay in three months."<br><br>I sat down on the rolling stool in the corner.<br><br>—<br><br>She pulled a discharge sheet off a clipboard and turned it over to the blank side. She put it on the counter. She drew a tube.<br><br>She said: "Your wife's colon is a muscle. To do its job, it has to contract. To contract, it needs fuel. The fuel is a class of molecules called short-chain fatty acids. SCFAs."<br><br>She tapped the drawing.<br><br>"SCFAs are made by two specific bacteria in your gut. Their names do not matter. Just remember there are two of them and they are the engine of her colon. When they are healthy, she goes once a day, no thinking about it. When they crash, she does not go for nine days, twelve days, sixteen days."<br><br>She kept going.<br><br>"Now here is what GLP-1 medications do to those bacteria. They starve them. The medication suppresses the things those bacteria feed on. By month six in most users, the populations are at a fraction of what they were before the medication started."<br><br>I felt the back of my neck get cold.<br><br>—<br><br>She pointed at the drawing again.<br><br>"When the bacteria crash, SCFA production crashes. Her colon loses the fuel it needs to contract. That is why she can drink three liters of water a day and still not go for twelve days. Water does not fuel a muscle."<br><br>I asked her about the fiber.<br><br>She actually shook her head when I said it.<br><br>She said: "Fiber is what those bacteria eat. If the bacteria are dead, the fiber does not get fermented. It just sits. It bulks up. In a slowed gut, it makes the problem worse. The Miralax in your wife's bathroom is the only thing that has been keeping her from being in this bay for the last four months. The fiber gummies have been making it worse the whole time."<br><br>She sat down across from me on a second stool.<br><br>"I am telling you this because most primary care doctors have not caught up to this yet. Your wife has been doing exactly what her doctor told her to do, and her doctor has been wrong, and the system is not currently set up to fix that for the next several years."<br><br>She looked me in the eye.<br><br>"You are going to have to fix it for her."<br><br>—<br><br>I want to write down what she said next, because I have it on the back of that discharge sheet and I have not thrown it away.<br><br>—<br><br>She said: "There are three things she needs to be taking. The Miralax is not on the list. She can still take it as a rescue if she has to. But it does not address the actual problem."<br><br>She wrote three things on the sheet.<br><br>"Postbiotics from fermentation. Not regular probiotics. Those are live bacteria that mostly die in stomach acid. Postbiotics are the molecular outputs of fermentation. They survive the trip and feed the right strains."<br><br>"Slippery elm. To soothe the lining of her colon, which is now inflamed from the chronic constipation and pressure. Slippery elm coats it while the bacteria reestablish."<br><br>"Dandelion root. To support the bile flow. That is part of what GLP-1 medications slow down, and it is part of why she has been having sulfur burps you have probably noticed."<br><br>I had noticed the burps. I had not asked about those either.<br><br>—<br><br>I asked her if there was a single product that had all three.<br><br>She paused.<br><br>She said: "I am not supposed to recommend specific brands. Pouch of sixty gummies, one a night, ninety minutes before bed. It has all three things in the dose ranges that work."<br><br>She handed me the discharge sheet.<br><br>She said: "Order it tonight. Start her on it the day she comes home. class="x14vqqas"><strong>Sponsored</strong></span><span><strong></strong></span></div></div></span></div></div></div></div></div><div class="x1plvlek xryxfnj"><div class="_7jyr _a25-"><span class="x8t9es0 xw23nyj xo1l8bm x63nzvj x108nfp6 xq9mrsl x1h4wwuj xeuugli"><div tabindex="0" role="button"><div class="_4ik4 _4ik5" style="line-height: 16px; max-height: 112px; -webkit-line-clamp: 7;"><div style="white-space: pre-wrap;"><span>I've been a colorectal surgeon for twelve years. And if you go days without a real bowel movement, you strain until you sweat, and your doctor keeps brushing you off with "more fiber, more water"... I'm about to tell you exactly what they're hiding from you, and why they'll NEVER tell you the truth.<br><br>And by the end of this, you're going to be pissed.<br><br>My name is Dr. Ellen Walsh. Board-certified colorectal surgeon. Twelve years operating on the lower gut. Published in Diseases of the Colon &amp; Rectum. More than four hundred colectomies.<br><br>And I'm breaking ranks with my own profession to tell you this.<br><br>Because there are three things happening right now.<br><br>One — your body is screaming at you that something is wrong.<br><br>Two — the medical system is gaslighting you into believing it's normal.<br><br>And three — there's a billion-dollar laxative industry that profits every single day you stay stuck.<br><br>So let me tell you what happened with one of my patients, because her story is going to open your eyes to how messed up this really is.<br><br>Her name is Denise. Fifty-one years old.<br><br>By the end of most weeks, she hadn't had a real bowel movement in eleven days. For six straight years.<br><br>She'd tried everything — every laxative on the shelf, the prescriptions, thousands of dollars in tests. Every one quit on her.<br><br>When something finally moved, it was hard little pebbles — and she strained so hard the hemorrhoids bled. Every single time.<br><br>Her stomach was so bloated by every evening she looked six months pregnant — she couldn't button the jeans she'd worn for a decade. She'd been an easy-going, regular person her whole life. Then, somewhere along the way, the urge to go just... switched off. "It's like my body forgot how," she told me.<br><br>She told me she'd stopped accepting dinner invitations — she couldn't sit through a meal with her stomach that tight. She'd stopped traveling. She'd given up most of the foods she loved, because every bite, she said, just made it worse.<br><br>And even on the rare day something came, she told me, she never felt empty — there was always more, just out of reach. She kept a plastic syringe in her bathroom drawer — some mornings she'd use it to flush herself out, because nothing else worked. Her husband thought she was just "getting older." But she told me, almost in tears, that some days she didn't feel like a person anymore.<br><br>And here's what makes me sick to my stomach:<br><br>I was the surgeon she was sent to.<br><br>Multiple doctors before me. Her GP. Her gastroenterologist. Then me — the colorectal surgeon. Thousands of dollars in appointments, scopes, blood work. And a colectomy referral with her name on it sitting on my desk.<br><br>And you know what every single one of us told her first?<br><br>"Your colonoscopy is clean."<br><br>"It's probably just IBS."<br><br>"It's normal as you get older."<br><br>"Take some MiraLAX."<br><br>"Eat more fiber."<br><br>"Drink more water."<br><br>DRINK MORE WATER. This woman hadn't gone in eleven days, and we were handing her a glass of water.<br><br>But here's where it gets worse — and this is the part that haunts me now.<br><br>We stacked her up. MiraLAX every day. Then magnesium on top. Then senna for when the magnesium quit working.<br><br>And the more she leaned on them, the less her body did on its own. The laxatives forced something through once. The next morning, she was just as stuck as the day before.<br><br>I watched this woman — who did everything we told her — get WORSE. Not better. Worse.<br><br>And for a long time, I didn't understand why.<br><br>Until I stopped being able to lie to myself. Because I had it too.<br><br>For twelve years I'd hidden the same thing Denise had — once every nine days, magnesium between cases, telling no one. I'd built a career cutting out colons like the one I was quietly wrecking in my own body. Every drug I'd handed my patients, I'd already failed on myself.<br><br>So I did the one thing I'd never let myself do as a working surgeon. I put down the drug-rep handouts and started reading the research nobody opens on the floor — the original motility studies, buried in the back of the journals.<br><br>And I kept hitting a wall.<br><br>The papers that seemed to matter weren't about stool, or fiber, or water. They kept circling back to one kind of cell in the colon wall — the cells that set its rhythm. I knew the name from med school. I'd never once tied them to a patient who couldn't go.<br><br>And one name was on half the papers I was reading. A Japanese gastroenterologist, Dr. Kenji Sato — thirty years on those exact cells.<br><br>So I did something I hadn't done since residency. I went and found the one person who could explain it to me.<br><br>That October there was an international gastroenterology conference in Kyoto, and his name was on the program. I skipped my own session to sit in the back of his.<br><br>Afterward I caught him at the coffee table, and I did something I'd never done at a conference. I told a stranger the truth about my own body.<br><br>He didn't look surprised. He asked me three questions — how often, since when, what I'd tried — and then he reached for a napkin.<br><br>"Your colon doesn't move on willpower," he said. "It moves when a set of pacemaker cells in the wall fire a contraction. They're called the interstitial cells of Cajal. When they fire, you feel the urge. When you lose them, the urge goes with them."<br><br>He drew them on the napkin — small, scattered through the muscle.<br><br>"In 2002, a paper in Gastroenterology counted these cells in the colons of people with severe constipation. They were physically depleted — fewer of them, in every layer. The field has known that for twenty years. What we didn't know was why."<br><br>He drew an arrow.<br><br>"Then we found it. A constipated colon runs two enzymes — NOX1 and DUOX2 — in overdrive. Their only job is to make free radicals. And free radicals corrode those pacemaker cells the way rust eats iron — slowly, from the inside. The cells barely regenerate. So you lose them, quietly, for years — while every colonoscopy comes back clean, because oxidation doesn't show up on a scan."<br><br>I sat there thinking about four hundred colectomies. About Denise. About the magnesium in my own locker.<br><br>"Then why has no one ever told me this?" I asked.<br><br>He smiled, not unkindly. "Because there's nothing in it to prescribe. People like me only ever see the end of it — on an operating table. By then nobody's asking what started it."<br><br>Then he told me the part that changed everything.<br><br>"But here's what I want you to hear," he said. "The damage is oxidative — and oxidation can be stopped. Last year a paper in Frontiers in Pharmacology showed that when you scavenge those free radicals with a strong enough antioxidant, the pacemaker cells still alive recover their function, and the colon starts moving again. You can't regrow the ones you've lost. But you can stop the burning, and let what's left fire."<br><br>I asked him the only thing left. "Stop it with what?"<br><br>"That's the harder part," he said. "Most antioxidants never reach the colon — absorbed or broken down long before they arrive. The strongest one we've measured that actually gets there intact isn't a pill. It's the acids fermentation produces. The complex you find concentrated in kombucha."<br><br>I almost laughed. Kombucha. The fizzy drink in the cooler at the health-food store. In what world does that fix a colon that's stopped on its own?<br><br>But he wasn't talking about the drink. And by the time I understood the difference, I'd stopped laughing.<br><br>I flew home with two things I couldn't stop turning over: what was actually wrecking these colons, and a fix I almost couldn't believe.<br><br>Because once I understood what was really happening, every dead end of the last twelve years made sense.<br><br>Fiber? Fiber is raw material for bacteria the modern gut had already starved out. So it just sat there and turned to gas. That's why "more fiber" made me — and most of the women I'd operated on — more bloated, not less. It does nothing about the damage.<br><br>Magnesium and MiraLAX? They pull water into the colon. Water on top of a trigger that can't fire. You end up wet, full, and still unable to go. Neither one touches a single free radical.<br><br>Senna, Dulcolax? They force a contraction by chemically irritating the colon. It works once. But it does nothing to stop the corrosion — so you're back the next day, needing a little more each time. You never proved your colon works. You proved it only moves when something forces it.<br><br>And the worst one. The colectomy. The operation I built my career on. It cuts out the corroded stretch. It does nothing to stop the damage from taking the next.<br><br>And here's the part that made my blood boil.<br><br>The system already knows all of this. It's sitting in the literature — Sato's field has been publishing it for two decades. But unless you're being prepped for surgery, no one in my profession gives it a second thought.<br><br>Why?<br><br>Because you can't write a prescription for an antioxidant from a fermented food. You can't patent it. There's no money in telling you how to stop the damage yourself.<br><br>There IS money in keeping you on MiraLAX, magnesium, and a prescription you refill for the rest of your life.<br><br>See how that works?<br><br>I added up once what twelve years of chasing this had cost me — the laxatives, the magnesium, the scans, the appointments. About thirteen thousand dollars, to end up exactly where I started. Every dollar of it forced or faked one bowel movement and bought one more day. Not one cent of it stopped the corrosion.<br><br>So I went looking for the kombucha Sato had pointed me to. And I learned fast why a drink was never going to do this.<br><br>The acids that do the work were undetectable in half the store bottles labs have tested. You'd have to drink several a day — and all that sugar — to reach what the research used. It's still fermenting in the bottle and in you, which is the gas and bloat you're trying to escape. And the part that matters most here: heat destroys the antioxidants. Pasteurize a bottle, leave it warm on a shelf, and you've cooked off the one thing that stops the oxidation. The drink was the wrong delivery entirely.<br><br>Sato had told me what to look for before I left that conference. He'd watched too many patients waste money on the wrong version. A real fix had to do three things.<br><br>1. Deliver a standardized, un-heated dose of that antioxidant acid complex, concentrated enough to reach the pacemaker cells in the colon wall and shield the ones still alive — instead of being broken down on the way, the way most antioxidants are.<br><br>2. Carry the two strains the constipation trials kept naming: L. plantarum, with its own trial for more frequent movements, and B. coagulans, with its own for faster transit.<br><br>3. Wake the urge back up and calm the inflamed lining feeding the oxidation: dandelion root and slippery elm.<br><br>So I went hunting for something that did all three. Most of what's sold for "gut health" fails at least one. I tested everything I could get my hands on.<br><br>Then I found it. A standardized dose of kombucha's organic-acid complex — acetic, gluconic, lactic, and the rare one, glucuronic acid, that you'll find almost nowhere else in food — concentrated, never heat-killed, paired with the two strains, the dandelion, and the slippery elm. One concentrated kombucha gummy a day.<br><br>It's called Jevawell.<br><br>One more thing, because if you've had this long enough you've thought it. "My gut already ferments everything. I'm bloated. I might have SIBO. More fermentation is the last thing I need."<br><br>Fair fear. The fermentation already happened — outside your body. Metamucil, psyllium, fiber gummies — those just made the bloat worse, though I didn't understand why yet. Magnesium citrate. Magnesium glycinate, which fogged my head and flattened my mood. Senokot. Dulcolax. Milk of Magnesia. Prune juice. Smooth Move tea. Align, the probiotic the pharmacy lady swore by, thirty dollars a month. And way in the back, the Triphala I'd ordered at two in the morning off a Reddit post that swore it fixed everything.<br><br>A whole drawer. And not one thing in it would stick. Every one of them worked for exactly one week. Then it stopped.<br><br>And here's the part nobody tells you. While my body forgot how to go, I built a whole second life around the not-going.<br><br>I never ate before I had to be anywhere. When you're already backed up, putting food on top of a stuck system just piles on more pressure, more bloat, that heavy, full, almost-sick feeling with nowhere to go. So on any morning I needed to feel like a person, I skipped breakfast. There was no joy in eating anymore, just the math of when will I pay for this. I mapped every outing around a bathroom. I packed a bag. If it wasn't planned around my gut, it didn't happen.<br><br>And so, slowly, things stopped happening.<br><br>I stopped hosting. The potlucks went to somebody else. I wore a cardigan everywhere to hide my middle, even in July, because I was so bloated 24/7 I'd convinced myself I was overweight — I wasn't, my belly was just hard and round and tight all the time. I moved my fitted clothes to the back of the closet. When people asked why I'd gone quiet, I blamed my back.<br><br>And I told myself the same story everybody told me. It's just menopause. Just getting older. Just the stress of retiring. A lot of women my age.<br><br>Ray said I was fine. Bev, my oldest friend, said everybody slows down. My own kids said, "Mom, you worry too much."<br><br>But I was the one inside this body. And I knew something was wrong.<br><br>I finally went to see Dr. Okafor, who I've gone to for years and genuinely like. She ran the bloodwork. Normal. I'd had a colonoscopy not long before — clean, nothing there. She was kind about it. And then she said the thing.<br><br>"A lot of women your age go through this, Lorrie. Let's keep an eye on it. More water, more fiber."<br><br>More water. I already drink my eight glasses a day. Sixty-four ounces, every day, for years. And more fiber was already making it worse. She offered to refer me to a GI specialist if it didn't settle, and I said no, I'd be fine, and I drove home and told myself I was being dramatic.<br><br>And then I did exactly what she'd unknowingly told me to. I reorganized my survival routine and ordered more supplements. I got better at coping with it. Like that was the goal now.<br><br>Now I want to tell you about the morning of Riley's recital. Riley is my granddaughter. She was four.<br><br>I was up at 6 a.m., on the cold bathroom floor, a heating pad on my belly, doing the thing I couldn't tell a living soul about for years.<br><br>I'd started carrying a small plastic syringe in my purse. Not for medicine. I'd fill it with lukewarm water and use it to flush myself out from below — to push out whatever stool was stuck — so I could feel safe leaving the house. It was the only way I could trust my own body enough to walk out the door.<br><br>That morning, on the floor, it didn't work. The recital was at nine.<br><br>I got dressed anyway. Put on the stretchy pants. Drove to the school. And I sat in the parking lot and could not make myself go in. I watched the other grandmothers walk in, and I pictured sitting in that little auditorium, packed in a row, bloated and clenched and trapped, no clean way to leave. And I just couldn't.<br><br>I missed Riley's recital. I sat in a car and missed it.<br><br>That night I told Ray everything. The syringe. The 16 days. The whole drawer. The routine I'd built so he wouldn't see. I'd never said any of it out loud to anyone.<br><br>And then I told him the part that scared me most. That I didn't feel like a human being anymore, because I couldn't go to the bathroom like everybody else. That I thought this was just who I was now, and I'd missed my granddaughter sing because of it.<br><br>Ray didn't tell me I was being dramatic. He didn't say more water. He just held onto me on the edge of the bed and let me say it.<br><br>And then, after a while, he said, "Lorrie. My sister Coraline went through something like this. Up in Augusta, a few years back. And she found a thing she takes now. You should call her."<br><br>I called Coraline the next morning.<br><br>Coraline is Ray's older sister, 64, a retired hospice nurse over in Augusta, Georgia. The kind of woman who's sat at the edge of a lot of beds and doesn't flinch at anything.<br><br>She let me talk. And then she said, "Can I tell you something, Lorrie? You don't have to take it as advice. You can just take it as a story."<br><br>So she told me hers. She'd lost the urge completely too. Years of it. She'd ended up disimpacting herself by hand, the thing you swear you'll never do. And she told me — quietly, the way nurses say the serious things — that her own gastro had warned her where it was all heading. Once the flushing quit holding, he'd said, the only thing left on the table was taking the colon out.<br><br>I asked her what that meant, exactly. It meant surgery. The colon gone, and a bag worn on the side of your body for good.<br><br>That's where this road runs out, she said. She'd gotten close enough to read the sign. But she'd turned off before it came to that.<br><br>And here's what she said next, and read it slowly, because it's the first thing in three years that made me feel like I wasn't crazy.<br><br>The thing that finally helped her wasn't another fiber. Wasn't another laxative. Wasn't another probiotic. "It was a fourth kind of thing, Lorrie. Something already fermented. Kombucha."<br><br>I'd never been told there was a fourth kind of thing.<br><br>And then she said the part that broke something open in me. "You're not broken, Lorrie. Your gut just went quiet."<br><br>This was something that got done to my body, she said. Not something wrong with me. After three years of "you're fine, eat more fiber," somebody was finally telling me the problem had a cause — and that I wasn't it.<br><br>I didn't sleep that night. I sat up reading until almost one in the morning, and for once I understood it. Let me give it to you the plain way Coraline gave it to me.<br><br>Your colon doesn't move on its own. It moves when it gets a signal — an actual chemical signal, made by the bacteria living in your gut.<br><br>When those bacteria ferment what you eat, they release tiny organic acids. And those acids are what tell the colon to contract. That contraction — that's the urge. That's the whole thing you feel when your body says it's time.<br><br>Now. Years of antibiotics, years of stress, and a normal American diet wipe out the bacteria that make that signal. For me, perimenopause was probably the last shove.<br><br>No bacteria, no acids. No acids, no signal. No signal, no urge.<br><br>That's why I'd "lost the urge." That's why my body "forgot how." My body wasn't broken. It had gone silent.<br><br>And suddenly the whole drawer made sense. Fiber needs those bacteria to do anything — when they're gone, it just sits there and piles up, which is exactly why it made me more bloated. MiraLAX never restored the signal; it dragged in water to force one flush, then it was done. The probiotics sent in a couple of strains that mostly washed right through. None of them gave my gut its voice back. They were never going to.<br><br>So why is the fermented thing different? Because kombucha is already fermented. The work happens in the brewing, outside the body. So it delivers the finished acids — acetic, lactic, and gluconic — that my own bacteria had stopped making.<br><br>Those acids land on the receptors lining the colon. Those cells release serotonin. class="x14vqqas"><strong>Sponsored</strong></span><span><strong></strong></span></div></div></span></div></div></div></div></div><div class="x1plvlek xryxfnj"><div class="_7jyr _a25-"><span class="x8t9es0 xw23nyj xo1l8bm x63nzvj x108nfp6 xq9mrsl x1h4wwuj xeuugli"><div tabindex="0" role="button"><div class="_4ik4 _4ik5" style="line-height: 16px; max-height: 112px; -webkit-line-clamp: 7;"><div style="white-space: pre-wrap;"><span>My father took MiraLAX for twelve years. His bowel movements were managed at every single checkup. When he died from complications of chronic constipation at 63, I asked his gastroenterologist how that was possible. What she told me changed everything I thought I knew about laxatives.<br><br>Because three months ago, I was standing in the same spot my father stood. Same laxative on the counter. Same doctor pushing it. And I almost filled the prescription without asking the one question that would have saved my father's life.<br><br>My constipation hit every 4-5 days between movements. My doctor didn't hesitate. "We've watched this long enough. I'm starting you on daily MiraLAX."<br><br>Eight minutes. That's how long the appointment lasted. She heard "constipated," wrote it down, and told me to come back in three months.<br><br>But my husband works in healthcare administration and he wouldn't let it go. "Your doctor checks whether you're going," he said. "That's output on a chart. A functional medicine specialist checks what's happening inside your gut. Those are two different things. Before you start that laxative, I want someone looking at what's actually broken."<br><br>The specialist spent an hour with me. Not eight minutes. She ran tests my regular doctor had never ordered — gut microbiome panel, bacterial diversity analysis, short-chain fatty acid production capacity, inflammatory markers. She checked things my gastroenterologist had never checked in six years of appointments.<br><br>When she came back with the results, she wasn't smiling.<br><br>"Your bowel frequency says every 4-5 days. That tells me one thing — the output is slow. But these tests tell me something your bowel frequency can't."<br><br>She turned the screen toward me. Graphs. Color-coded charts. Bacterial population data.<br><br>"These are your short-chain fatty acid producers. Faecalibacterium. Bifidobacterium. The bacteria that ferment fiber into the chemical signals that tell your colon to contract."<br><br>She pointed at a range on the chart. "A healthy woman your age should be here."<br><br>She pointed at another range. Much lower. "You're here. I normally see this level of depletion in patients who've been on daily laxatives for years. You haven't started yet. Your bacteria collapsed from diet, stress, and aging alone."<br><br>I stared at her. "But my doctor said the constipation was the problem. If we force a movement with MiraLAX—"<br><br>"The constipation is the last thing to change," she said. "Your gut bacteria have been declining for years — probably more than a decade — before your bowel movements started slowing. The constipation your doctor is reacting to? That's the end of the process. Not the beginning."<br><br>She let that settle.<br><br>"Think about it. Your constipation didn't jump to every 5 days overnight. It crept. Every 2 days became 3. Then 4. Then 5. Over years. Your doctor watched it worsen and said 'eat more fiber' until it crossed a threshold. Then she reached for MiraLAX."<br><br>"But what was happening inside your gut during those years? The bacterial collapse was already well underway. The depleted microbiome I'm measuring today didn't start when you hit 5 days. It started a decade before that."<br><br>"Your bowel frequency is the surface," she said. "What I'm seeing underneath it is ten years ahead of what that number suggests."<br><br>I felt sick. "So what does MiraLAX do?"<br><br>She was direct.<br><br>"MiraLAX pulls water into your colon through osmosis. Waste moves from bulk pressure — not because your muscles contracted. Your doctor sees you went and says 'working well, keep taking it.'"<br><br>She paused.<br><br>"But it doesn't restore your gut bacteria. It doesn't rebuild the fermentation that produces your signal. It doesn't address the reason your colon muscles lost the signal to contract on their own. The output improves. The bacterial ecosystem — what I'm seeing on these tests — continues to decline. And every dose flushes out more of the bacteria you need."<br><br>She looked at me. "The laxative is like repainting a house with a crumbling foundation. From the outside, everything looks fine. You're going. But the structure underneath keeps collapsing."<br><br>And that's when I understood what happened to my father.<br><br>He'd been on MiraLAX for twelve years. Started at 62 — one capful daily. His doctor called it "the gold standard for chronic constipation." Said it was gentle. Non-habit forming. He'd probably need it long-term, but that was fine.<br><br>The dependency came within the first year. Not dramatic. Gradual. He'd take it, go regularly. Miss a day, nothing moved. "I guess I just need it consistently now."<br><br>By year three, one capful wasn't enough. His doctor increased to two. "Your body adjusted. Totally normal."<br><br>By year five, they added magnesium citrate three times a week. "Just to keep things moving."<br><br>And the bloating. God, the bloating.<br><br>This was a man who used to build furniture in his garage. Who coached my brother's football team. Who grilled for the whole neighborhood on the Fourth of July.<br><br>By 65, his stomach swelled up every afternoon like he was carrying a basketball. He stopped tucking in his shirts. Stopped wearing belts. Just loose pants and flannel shirts buttoned over that distended belly.<br><br>The brain fog crept in around year four. Forgetting things. Losing conversations mid-sentence. Falling asleep at the table. My mother would cover him with a blanket on the couch at 7 PM and eat dinner alone.<br><br>The exhaustion was relentless. Not tiredness — poisoning. His kidneys and liver working overtime to process toxins his gut should have eliminated but couldn't.<br><br>He died at 63. Bowel obstruction. Impaction that had been building for months behind the managed output. Perforation. Sepsis.<br><br>Twelve years of managed movements. Twelve years of escalating doses. Twelve years of his doctor saying "the MiraLAX is working."<br><br>And he died of the thing they were managing.<br><br>I told the specialist. She was quiet.<br><br>"That's unfortunately common," she said. "The laxative managed his output for twelve years. But the bacterial collapse — the root cause — continued the entire time. His gut looked like it was working. The bacteria producing the signal were dying underneath. That's the gap the laxative can't close."<br><br>There it was. The answer to the question I'd carried since I was 41 years old, standing in a hospital hallway being told my father was gone.<br><br>His output was managed for twelve years. And he still died of the thing the laxative was supposed to prevent.<br><br>Now a specialist was telling me why.<br><br>"So what do I do?" I asked. "Is the laxative the only option?"<br><br>She said I had two paths.<br><br>Path one: start the MiraLAX. The output improves. Going more frequently at every checkup. "But the bacterial collapse continues underneath," she said. "And over time, the dose increases. Maybe magnesium added. Stimulant laxatives eventually. The output stays managed. The foundation keeps dying."<br><br>Path two: actually address why my gut bacteria are depleted.<br><br>"How?" I asked.<br><br>She explained:<br><br>Your colon doesn't move waste automatically. It relies on chemical signals — short-chain fatty acids, the molecules your gut bacteria make when they ferment fiber. When those bacteria are healthy, those acids bind the receptors on your colon wall and tell the muscles to contract. Waste moves through naturally.<br><br>But when those bacteria are depleted, the signal dies. Your colon muscles sit there. Capable. But silent.<br><br>"When that signal disappears," she said, "your colon stops contracting on its own. Waste doesn't move. That's what constipation IS — not a stool problem, but a signaling problem."<br><br>"MiraLAX forces the output through water pressure," she said. "The frequency improves on paper. But it doesn't restore the bacteria, and it doesn't put those signaling molecules back. It flushes out more bacteria with every dose. Your gut becomes dependent on the chemical bypass instead of recovering its own function."<br><br>"Your father was on that bypass for twelve years. His output was managed. His bacteria kept dying. The laxative was managing him. It wasn't healing him."<br><br>Managing. Not healing.<br><br>That's what my father was for twelve years.<br><br>"Is there a way to actually restore the signal?" I asked.<br><br>She said the problem isn't only the missing bacteria — it's the missing molecules they used to make. And the most direct way to put those molecules back isn't a fiber you hope your damaged gut can still ferment. It's a postbiotic. Something already fermented.<br><br>"Like what?" I asked.<br><br>"Kombucha," she said. "Properly concentrated. Not the bottled sugar-water at the grocery store."<br><br>I almost laughed. "Kombucha? My doctor wants me on MiraLAX and you're telling me about kombucha?"<br><br>She pulled up research on her screen. "Fiber asks your gut to make those short-chain fatty acids from scratch. But your bacteria are too depleted to do it — that's the whole problem. Kombucha is pre-fermented. The organic acids are already made. Acetic, lactic, gluconic — the same family of molecules your missing bacteria used to produce. They hit the same receptors on your colon wall. They send the same signal."<br><br>"It's the same target the laxative aims at — getting your gut to move. But instead of chemically forcing your colon every 24 hours, the fermentation acids restore the signal naturally. And the live cultures rebuild the bacteria that make your own signal again. You're rebuilding the function, not replacing it."<br><br>She showed me the studies. A 2024 human trial where kombucha consumption measurably enriched the short-chain-fatty-acid-producing bacteria — including the exact spore strain, Bacillus coagulans, that has its own constipation trials. Another where that strain cut colonic transit time in eight weeks. Another where Lactobacillus plantarum improved spontaneous bowel movements over six weeks.<br><br>But — she held up a finger — most kombucha is useless for this.<br><br>Bottled kombucha is mostly sugar, water, and carbonation. The live cultures are often killed in pasteurization and the active acids are present in trace amounts. Apple cider vinegar gummies have a single acid and nothing living. The fermentation matrix that actually does the work has to be concentrated, daily-dosed, and paired with the two strains that have real constipation trials behind them — L. plantarum and B. coagulans — plus a prebiotic to feed them and a soother for the gut wall.<br><br>She said most "gut health" gummies on the market are the equivalent of a splash of vinegar in a sugar bath. Below the threshold. The math doesn't work.<br><br>So I started looking. Most were garbage. Pasteurized. Underdosed. Wrong formulation.<br><br>First brand — the bottled kombucha everyone drinks, from the grocery store. Six weeks, two bottles a day. Nothing changed except the bloating got worse. Checked the label: more sugar than a soda, cultures cooked out in pasteurization.<br><br>Second brand — apple cider vinegar gummies, "gut reset." Eight weeks. Nothing. One acid, no live strains.<br><br>Third brand — a "probiotic" gummy from the supplement store, most expensive on the shelf. Four weeks. Still going every 4-5 days. Single strain, no fermentation matrix at all.<br><br>I was running out of time. My follow-up with my regular doctor was three weeks away. She was going to ask if I'd started the MiraLAX.<br><br>After the third brand failed, I found Jevawell.
