I know I was. I'm still a little pissed at myself.\n\nMy name is Dr. Ellen Walsh. Board-certified colorectal surgeon. Twelve years operating on the lower gut. Fellowship-trained at one of the busiest colorectal programs in the country. Seventy-one colectomies.\n\nAnd I'm breaking ranks with my own profession to tell you this.\n\nBecause there are three things I need you to understand, and they all point at the same place.\n\nOne \u2014 your body is screaming at you that something is wrong, and it's right.\n\nTwo \u2014 there is a real, specific cause for it, and it has a name.\n\nAnd three \u2014 there is exactly one reason you have never heard that name from a doctor. With my own career. Stay with me.\n\nSo let me tell you what happened with one of my patients, because her story is going to open your eyes to how this actually works.\n\nHer name is Denise. Fifty-one years old.\n\nFor YEARS \u2014 and I mean six straight years \u2014 she had been dealing with this.\n\nHer stomach? Bloated so hard by every evening she looked six months pregnant. She couldn't button the jeans she'd worn for a decade. He died the spring our youngest started kindergarten.\n\nThe year before, he'd started saying his belly felt tight. He was 65. His GP said keep up the MiraLAX, maybe add a little Metamucil. He did. He did exactly what they told him.\n\nThe week he died, I didn't know how bad it had gotten. He hadn't told my mother. He hadn't told me.\n\nThe death certificate said complications from chronic constipation. I didn't understand what that meant. On the flight home from the funeral I made myself read the discharge summary, word by word, until I did.\n\nA stool impaction had blocked his bowel. It sat there long enough that the wall tore. The infection went into his blood. Sepsis. I didn't believe it either, until I read it in a hospital's own words.\n\nEvery test he ever took came back normal.\n\nHe died of the thing they were managing.\n\nThe MiraLAX had shown up on his counter the year I turned 30. His GP had a line for it.\n\n\"This is your new best friend now.\"\n\nMy father wrote it down on a Post-it inside the kitchen cabinet. His engineer's block letters. NEW BEST FRIEND. I only went when I made myself go.\n\nThe bloat showed up at 8 PM like a guest who wouldn't leave. I stopped wearing the wrap dress because I looked six months pregnant by dinner. Four months of chalky nightly chugs. Quit working after three rounds.\n\nCastor oil. Once. Three hours of cramping for ten minutes of release. Never again.\n\nAlign. Probiotics. Next to my keys. Folded once down the middle. I walked past it every morning on my way to the coffee pot and pretended I wasn't seeing it.\n\nI'm 49. I live alone. There is no one else in this house to ask me what the prescription is for or why I haven't filled it.\n\nThat part matters.\n\nMy mother was a quiet woman.\n\nShe worked thirty-one years at the same regional bank. She wore the same gold cross around her neck every day of her adult life. She made coffee at 5:45 in the morning, before her shift, in the same blue mug with the chipped handle.\n\nI was twenty-eight the first time I saw the white powder go into her cup.\n\n\"My doctor said this is my new best friend now.\"\n\nThat was the phrase. Verbatim. She said it the way you say something you've decided not to question.\n\nShe used MiraLAX in her coffee \u2014 not orange juice, she didn't like sweet things in the morning \u2014 every day for fifteen years.\n\nI visited every other Sunday. I watched her scoop the powder from the kitchen table. After a few years I stopped looking at it. After a few more, I stopped asking.\n\n\"I'm regular as a clock,\" she'd say.\n\nShe said it like a small reassurance. The way you tell a child a story is over and they don't have to worry anymore.\n\nThe last three years of her life she started saying her belly felt \"full all the time.\"\n\nShe was sixty-five.\n\nHer GP added Metamucil to the MiraLAX. He didn't run a single panel. He said \"at your age, this is what we manage.\"\n\nThe week she died I was at a work conference in Charlotte. I hadn't called Sunday.\n\nShe went to the ER on Tuesday feeling tight. They admitted her Wednesday. By Thursday morning she was on a ventilator. She died Friday afternoon.\n\nThe discharge summary said: sepsis secondary to fecal impaction with bowel wall compromise.\n\nI had to look up what \"fecal impaction\" meant on my phone, standing in the hospital parking lot, in the August heat.\n\nThat was two summers ago. The August it didn't rain once.\n\nMy own constipation started around the time I turned forty-two.\n\nSubtle at first. Every other day became every third. Every third became every fifth. By forty-five I was going every five or six days at best.\n\nBy forty-seven I had stopped saying it out loud, to anyone, including myself.\n\nYou learn to live around it.\n\nYou learn which skirts not to wear because by six in the evening you look six months pregnant. You learn which side of the closet to push toward. You buy three long cardigans on a Saturday and tell yourself you just like cardigans now.\n\nYou sit on the toilet for an hour with your knees pulled up and your eyes closed and your phone face-down on the floor. You learn to listen for your downstairs neighbor's TV through the floor so the silence doesn't feel quite so loud.\n\nYou pass rabbit-pellet stools.\n\nYou see blood on the paper on a Tuesday and you go to work anyway.\n\nYou stop telling your friends. You stop telling your sister. You stop telling your GP after the third visit because each time he said \"more fiber, more water, more walking\" and you wanted to put your head on his desk and cry.\n\nYou start dreading meals because eating is just the front end of the same long question \u2014 when will I poop?\n\nYou stop having a body that feels like yours.\n\nAnd every time you describe one of these things to yourself, even silently, in your own kitchen, alone, you see a flash of your mother doing the same thing.\n\nHer hand on her lower belly at nine PM watching the news.\n\nThe gold cross flat on a swollen stomach.\n\nThe blue mug. The white powder.\n\nI'm fine.\n\nShe said I'm fine for fifteen years.\n\nI'm saying it now to no one, because no one is in the room to ask.\n\nI had a drawer.\n\nAfter my mother died, six months later, the following February, I drove to her apartment to clean it out. I'd put it off twice. My ex-husband would've helped me three years before that. He wasn't around for this one.\n\nI went alone.\n\nI emptied the kitchen. The bedroom. The hall closet. The little desk by the window where she paid her bills with a pen that had her name engraved on it.\n\nThen I opened the bathroom cabinet.\n\nThree unopened MiraLAX packets on the top shelf.\n\nHalf a bottle of magnesium citrate.\n\nA blister pack of Dulcolax.\n\nA box of senna tablets.\n\nA jar of prune juice in the fridge two feet away, cream and white label, three quarters full.\n\nI stood there with my hand on the cabinet door for a long time.\n\nBecause that cabinet was my cabinet.\n\nItem for item.\n\nI had built it for seven years without seeing it.\n\nI closed the door. Sat on the edge of the tub. Drove home that night with her gold cross in my pocket because I couldn't make myself wear it. Booked an appointment with my own GP the next morning.\n\nThis is what was in my drawer, that February, on the morning I sat on my bathroom floor with the door open and counted.\n\nMiraLAX \u2014 the white powder, my doctor's \"new best friend.\"\n\nMetamucil \u2014 two orange tubs stacked.\n\nMagnesium citrate \u2014 the green-and-yellow soda bottle. Tastes like grapefruit lighter fluid. I chugged it Sunday nights.\n\nMagnesium glycinate \u2014 the calmer one. Made me sleepy. Didn't move anything.\n\nSenna tablets \u2014 the brown ones. \"The whip,\" I called them. For Mondays before a Tuesday flight.\n\nDulcolax suppositories \u2014 the box in the back. The emergency drawer.\n\nMilk of Magnesia \u2014 four months of chalky nightly chugs. Huge bloated belly. Stopped working after three rounds.\n\nCastor oil \u2014 three days. The smell. Three hours of cramping for ten minutes of release. Gave up.\n\nAlign \u2014 I fell for Align. Thirty a month for five months. Two good weeks, then nothing.\n\nSmooth Move tea \u2014 the kettle on at nine PM every Sunday.\n\nPrune juice \u2014 every morning until I gagged at the sight of the bottle.\n\nTriphala \u2014 three weeks of working, then nothing.\n\nFiber gummies \u2014 two brands. Made the bloat worse.\n\nA squatty potty under the sink.\n\nA colonoscopy at forty-three. \"Nothing remarkable. Mild slow transit, common at your age.\"\n\nA pelvic-floor PT referral I canceled twice and never went to.\n\nSix sessions with an acupuncturist because a coworker swore by it.\n\nI sat there on the tile and I thought: Item for item.\n\nMy cabinet is my mother's cabinet.\n\nI have been becoming her in this bathroom for seven years and no one was here to see it.\n\nI went to my GP the week of the first frost. Last month.\n\nHe's been my GP for four years. Same practice as my mother's old doctor. New office building. Same wallpaper, almost.\n\nHe listened for eight minutes.\n\nHe said, \"You've tried a lot. Let's just put you on a daily MiraLAX. It'll be your new best friend.\"\n\nThe exact phrase.\n\nI drove home with the prescription in my purse. Put it on the kitchen counter next to my keys.\n\nI didn't fill it that day.\n\nI didn't fill it the next day.\n\nI didn't fill it the day after.\n\nIt sat there for nine days.\n\nOn the ninth night I poured a glass of wine after work and walked into the kitchen.\n\nI stood at the counter and looked at the folded paper.\n\nThen I walked into the bathroom and opened the drawer.\n\nThen I walked back into the kitchen and opened my phone.\n\nI searched: why did my mother die of constipation.\n\nI read for two hours.\n\nI learned what fecal impaction does to a colon wall over fifteen years. I learned about bacterial dysbiosis. I learned the word butyrate. I learned that eighty percent of people with slow transit don't respond to more fiber, and I read it three times because no doctor had ever said it to me out loud.\n\nI did not sleep.\n\nAt one forty-five in the morning I searched: integrative medicine constipation near me.\n\nThe first result was a clinic two blocks from where my mother had spent her final five days. A hospice-adjacent integrative medicine clinic in a single-story brick building with a wheelchair ramp.\n\nI'd driven past it. I remembered thinking it looked like a yoga studio.\n\nI called them at eight the next morning before I let myself talk myself out of it. The intake was two hundred and sixty dollars. The first available appointment was two weeks out.\n\nI took it.\n\nI almost canceled it twice.\n\nTwo hundred and sixty dollars and a stranger's intake form asking about my mother's medical history felt, for about an hour on a Thursday afternoon, like grief tourism. Like I was being dramatic. Like my GP's prescription on the counter was probably fine and I was making a movie out of my own life because I was lonely.\n\nI went anyway.\n\nThe waiting room smelled like cedar.\n\nThere was a salt lamp on the front desk. A basket of fleece blankets by the window. Someone offered me chamomile tea. I almost cried before I sat down.\n\nThe intake form was eight pages.\n\nOn page three it asked: Has anyone in your immediate family had unexplained bowel complications?\n\nThat was when I cried in a doctor's office for the first time in twenty years.\n\nHer name was Naomi Whitfield. PA-C. Late forties. Black, locs pulled back, a linen blazer thrown over scrubs. No white coat. She came out to the waiting room herself \u2014 no medical assistant \u2014 and said, \"I read your intake form. I'm so sorry about your mother. Come sit down.\"\n\nHer consult room had been the building's library, she told me. Wood shelves still on the walls. A reading lamp in the corner. A long oak table instead of an exam bed. She had spent fifteen years in oncology palliative care before this. She said it like an apology for understanding what I'd put on page three.\n\nThe first thing she did was order a microbiome panel and an inflammation panel.\n\n\"I want to see what's actually under the symptom before we touch the symptom.\"\n\nTwo hundred and ninety dollars. Out of pocket. Before we look at any of the numbers.\"\n\nShe leaned forward.\n\n\"For fifteen years, what we did with your mother \u2014 what we did with everyone in your mother's generation \u2014 was re-shingle the roof every year while the beams rotted underneath. From the street, the house looked fine. The shingles were clean. The shutters were painted. The output was managed.\"\n\n\"But the beams \u2014 the bacterial signaling architecture that holds the whole structure up \u2014 those beams collapsed quietly for fifteen years. By the time the ceiling caved in, no one knew where to look.\"\n\nI wrote that down. On a napkin. With a pen I borrowed from her.\n\nThen she walked through the panel.\n\nShe pointed at the first bar on the chart.\n\n\"Bifidobacterium. Top-three population in a healthy colon. Yours is in the bottom fifteen percent. These are the bacteria that ferment fiber into the chemical signals that tell your colon muscles when to contract. Without them, the muscles are getting no signal.\"\n\nShe pointed at the second.\n\n\"Akkermansia muciniphila. Should be at three to five percent. Yours is at zero point three. These are the bacteria that maintain the mucus layer that lines and protects your gut wall. When they're gone, the wall thins. Stool sits there longer. The mucus dries out. Every day on a laxative without restoring the Akkermansia is a day the wall keeps thinning.\"\n\nShe pointed at the third.\n\n\"Faecalibacterium prausnitzii. Should be five to ten percent. Yours is at zero point six. These produce butyrate. The most important short-chain fatty acid for colon-wall health and motility signaling.\"\n\nShe set the pen down.\n\n\"Short-chain fatty acids \u2014 butyrate, acetate, propionate \u2014 are the chemical signals the bacteria send the colon muscles to tell them when to contract. Your mother's muscles weren't broken. They just weren't getting the signal. For fifteen years.\"\n\nI said, \"My GP told me more fiber \u2014\"\n\nShe interrupted me. Kindly.\n\n\"Fiber is the raw material. If the bacteria that ferment it aren't there, more fiber is more lumber stacked on a foundation that can't hold it. About eighty percent of people with what you have don't respond to more fiber. That's published. That's not me being clever.\"\n\nShe kept going.\n\n\"And before you ask about probiotics. Most probiotics deliver one or two strains that show up, play for a week, and pass through. Like one violinist on an empty stage. What you actually need is fermentation. The pre-finished postbiotic byproducts the bacteria make \u2014 delivered daily, the way your grandmother got them from kombucha, kefir, fermented vegetables, sauerkraut. That is a different category. That is what your mother never got. Your grandmother probably did, daily, without ever knowing why.\"\n\nThen she said the line about MiraLAX.\n\n\"MiraLAX is polyethylene glycol. An osmotic agent. It pulls water into the colon. It does not feed bacteria. It does not restore the architecture. It does not lay one new beam. It is re-shingling. Fifteen years of re-shingling is what we saw in your mother's discharge summary.\"\n\nShe paused.\n\nShe looked at me directly.\n\n\"You are not your mother. You're sitting here. She didn't get this conversation. You are.\"\n\nI wrote that down too. Seven days where I go to the bathroom like a normal person \u2014 no straining, no waiting, no bloating up by lunch. And every single time, I let myself believe eleven years of constipation are finally over.\n\nNobody warns you the good weeks are the cruelest part. The bad weeks, you brace for. The good weeks lie. They whisper, maybe you imagined it. Maybe your body's fine.\n\nThen comes a Tuesday where I'm kneeling on the bathroom floor at 6 a.m., heating pad on my belly, a plastic syringe of warm water in my hand \u2014 flushing myself out by hand just so I'll feel safe leaving the house. And the good week is gone like it was never real.\n\nMy name is Maureen. Most of my life I've thought of myself as Carol's little sister. Carol taught me to drive. And Carol is the reason I finally stopped pretending this was normal \u2014 I'll get to that.\n\nI work part-time at the community college library here in Athens, Georgia, and I run a memoir circle on Thursdays \u2014 older folks writing their lives down before they forget them.\n\nIt started on a single Sunday in 2013. I can name the day. That morning everything worked the way it had my whole life. By that evening it just... stopped. And eleven years later my body still hasn't remembered how.\n\nAt first I thought it would pass. It didn't pass. It just got quieter and meaner.\n\nBy the end I was going once every two weeks. Sometimes longer. In between, I was bloated every hour of every day \u2014 not \"big dinner\" bloated, but hard and round and tight, the kind where you press your stomach and it doesn't give back. By noon I looked five months along. I'm not saying that for effect; a woman in my Thursday circle once smiled at my middle and asked when I was due. That's why there's a cardigan on the back of my chair \u2014 not for the draft. To hold over my stomach in the afternoons.\n\nBut the part that scared me most wasn't the bloating or the waiting. It was that I'd lost the urge completely. Not the pain \u2014 the signal. My body had stopped telling me it was time at all. I'd sit there out of habit, hoping, and nothing. Like a wire had been cut.\n\nSo I went looking for that wire myself.\n\nI took MiraLAX every morning with my coffee. Religiously.\n\nI drank my eight glasses of water a day. Sixty-four ounces, measured, every day, for years. If anyone ever told me to \"drink more water,\" I could have handed them the log.\n\nEighteen grams of fiber at breakfast alone.\n\nI quietly moved my fitted clothes to the back of the closet and stopped buying anything with a waistband.\n\nAnd I started dreading food. When you haven't gone in twelve days, every meal just piles onto a system that's already stuck \u2014 more bloat, more pressure, that full, heavy, almost sick feeling with nowhere for any of it to go. So I'd skip dinner before any morning I needed to feel halfway human. Eating became something I rationed.\n\nI dropped the Thursday circle from ninety minutes to forty-five, and told everyone my back was acting up.\n\nNothing dramatic. Just everything.\n\nNine days between movements. Then, after a year, fourteen.\n\nAnd there's a drawer in my kitchen I want you to picture, because I think a lot of you have one.\n\nMiraLAX. Metamucil. Magnesium citrate. Senokot. Dulcolax. Smooth Move tea. Psyllium. Prune juice. A box of Align that cost me thirty dollars a month for a while. Culturelle behind that.\n\nA whole drawer of things that worked for exactly one week.\n\nNow. The reason I keep coming back to Carol.\n\nCarol has the same thing I do. Her whole life. The same drawer of laxatives. The same \"just eat more fiber\" from every doctor she ever sat in front of. We used to joke about it on the phone like it was a family heirloom.\n\nBut Carol is eight years older than me. Eight years further down this same road.\n\nA few years back, the flushing \u2014 the exact thing I now do on my bathroom floor \u2014 stopped working for her. Her gut had slowed down so far that her doctor sat her down and told her to start getting acquainted with the idea of a colectomy. Surgery to take her colon out. A bag on her side for the rest of her life.\n\nThat's where this road ends if it keeps going. Not a vague someday. A surgeon, and a bag, and my big sister crying in her car.\n\nThat was the dread I carried every day. Because I knew I was only eight years behind her.\n\nI did go to my doctor about the constipation. Of course I did. Dr. Pruitt. Three years of fifteen-minute slots.\n\nVisit one: \"More fiber. More water. Try Metamucil.\" I rolled my eyes in the parking lot.\n\nVisit two, a year later, going once every nine days: \"MiraLAX is going to be your new best friend.\"\n\nVisit three, once every fourteen days now, the gastro referral still eleven months out: \"Let's keep an eye on it. I said something about too much barbecue. I finished the session. I drove home.\n\nAnd that night I did the thing the morning had been promising.\n\nOn the bathroom floor, with the plastic syringe and the warm water, flushing myself out by hand just so I'd feel safe leaving the house the next day. The seemingly nasty, horrendous, what-the-hell-has-my-life-come-to act that I have never said out loud to one living person.\n\nI caught my own face in the chrome of the tub.\n\nAnd I thought about Carol. When those bacteria ferment what I eat, they release tiny acids, and those acids are what tell the colon to contract. That's the urge. That's the whole thing.\n\nAnd mine were gone. Years of antibiotics, stress, the standard American diet had wiped out the bacteria that make the signal. No bacteria, no acids. No acids, no signal. No signal, no urge. That's why I'd stopped feeling the need to go at all. My body wasn't broken. It had gone silent.\n\nI read that and I sat back in my chair.\n\nEleven years.
